Compute Aligned Training:
Optimizing for Test Time Inference

Adam Ousherovitch Affiliation: Department of Statistics
University of Michigan
{aoushero, tewaria}@umich.edu    Ambuj Tewari Affiliation: Department of Statistics
University of Michigan
{aoushero, tewaria}@umich.edu
August 24, 2026
Abstract

Scaling test-time compute has emerged as a powerful mechanism for enhancing Large Language Model (LLM) performance. However, standard post-training paradigms, Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning (RL), optimize the likelihood of individual samples under a base policy, creating a misalignment with test time procedures that rely on aggregated or filtered outputs. In this work, we propose Compute Aligned Training, which aligns training objectives with test-time strategies. By conceptualizing inference strategies as operators on the base policy, we derive new loss functions that maximize performance when said strategies are applied. We instantiate such loss functions for SFT and RL across common test time strategies. Finally, we provide empirical evidence that this training method substantially improves test time scaling over standard training.

1 Introduction

In his foundational essay, The Bitter Lesson, Richard Sutton observed that "search and learning are the two most important classes of techniques for utilizing massive amounts of computation in AI research" [1]. Historically, the generative AI community has leaned heavily into the latter, driving progress by scaling the learning phase [2]. Recently, the frontier is shifting towards scaling test-time compute [3]: a form of search. Yet, current training paradigms treat learning and search as isolated, optimizing models for one-shot performance rather than operating in conjunction with a search procedure. However, ultimately, search and learning are not isolated processes. They complement each other in a continuous cycle. Search explores the environment to find high-quality answers, and learning internalizes these discoveries, enabling the model to search more effectively in the future. Therefore, learning benefits from a model optimized for search. Thus, to fully align with modern deployment, a model must be trained to support the inference procedures used at test-time.

Standard training, such as Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning (RL), explicitly optimizes for the expected reward of a single output. This implicitly encourages the model to converge on a narrow set of "safe," high-likelihood outputs. This misalignment is actively detrimental to test-time scaling – specifically, in the setting of using Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate multiple candidate solutions, particularly Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning traces [4], and applying aggregation strategies like Pass@NN [5], Majority Vote [6], or Best-of-NN verification [7]. Strategies like Best-of-NN and Pass@NN allow the model to benefit when it produces low-probability yet high-quality solutions. Standard training has been shown to actively degrade Pass@NN performance by effectively collapsing the exploration required for search [8, 9]. Similarly, Dang et al. [10] found that SFT can yield suboptimal test-time scaling under majority vote. The model is optimized for single output performance, so at inference, when it is forced to act as an ensemble, it performs suboptimally.

Despite the relevance of test-time strategies, standard training protocols remain largely agnostic to how models are actually deployed. Prior work has only identified and addressed isolated instances of this misalignment. Solutions are typically restricted to either a certain test time strategy or training modality (Section 1.1). However, this misalignment is a general phenomenon that persists across broad training paradigms, from SFT to RL and various test-time strategies. This raises the question, can we extract better performance under test time scaling by aligning training with test time strategy without substantially increasing training-time compute costs? Solving a problem this broad requires a generalized, rather than piecemeal, approach. To that end, we provide a unified theoretical framework as the mechanism to bridge the gap between training and inference.

In this work, we propose Compute Aligned Training (CAT), a framework for aligning training objectives with test-time. The key observation enabling this method is that the inputs to inference strategies are the generative model and a set of known hyperparameters, ultimately outputting a single solution. Thus, we can conceptualize inference strategies not as heuristics applied post-hoc, but as operators 𝒯\mathcal{T} that transform the base policy πθ\pi_{\theta} into an effective test-time distribution π~θ\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}. By performing gradient descent to minimize the loss with respect to this transformed distribution, we can align the model training with its deployment environment. Whether for SFT or RL, CAT re-weights gradients based on the "marginal utility" of a sample to the aggregate outcome with no added overhead. We will show empirically that this approach broadly improves performance under test-time scaling.

1.1 Related Works

Efforts to align training objectives with inference strategies have largely been fragmented across different modalities.

In the domain of Supervised Fine-Tuning, Chen et al. [8] pioneered the identification of the misalignment between Cross-Entropy and Pass@NN, proposing Direct Coverage Optimization (DCO). While the most foundational paper to our work, DCO is restricted to SFT and does not extend to strategies outside of Pass@NN. Our primary contribution is extending their ideas across Test Time Strategies, to RL, and beyond LLMs.

In the Reinforcement Learning setting, Tang et al. [11] propose gradient estimators for Pass@kk and Majority Voting. However, their method operates on a fundamentally different mechanism which introduces issues that CAT avoids (Appendix G). Alternatively, Chow et al. [12] addresses Best-of-NN for both SFT and RL, but relies on variational approximations of the verification process rather than exact policy optimization.

We propose a unified framework that overcomes these modality and efficiency constraints. Our operator-based formulation allows for computationally efficient, exact gradient scaling. This allows us to recover DCO as a special case while generalizing to RL and complex strategies beyond Pass@N.

1.2 Contributions

Our primary contributions are as follows:

  • •

    A Unified Operator Framework: We formalize test-time strategies as operators on the base policy, deriving a unified gradient scaling mechanism that aligns training objectives with arbitrary inference strategies. We then instantiate that framework for common cases in which it may be used.

  • •

    Empirical Validation across Paradigms: We provide empirical evidence that CAT generalizes the work of Chen et al. [8] in three directions. We push test time alignment to strategies beyond Pass@N, beyond SFT, and beyond LLMs to Protein Language Models (PLMs), successfully improving performance once an inference strategy is aligned.

2 Method: Compute Aligned Training

As shown in Chen et al. [8] and Yue et al. [9], the mismatch between training and inference decreases performance under test time scaling. The mechanism via which this happens is that standard objectives like Cross-Entropy optimize the likelihood of a sample regardless of whether that improvement actually changes the test-time outcome. This can cause effective overtraining once the Test Time Strategy (TTS) is applied.

Consider two scenarios that highlight this inefficiency:

  1. 1.

    The Efficiency Gap (Pass@NN): If a model has a 50%50\% probability of generating the correct answer (p=0.5p=0.5), increasing this to 90%90\% provides negligible benefit to a Pass@100 metric, where success is already virtually guaranteed. Yet, standard SFT continues to direct the model to maximize this likelihood.

  2. 2.

    The Consensus Gap (Majority Vote): Majority Vote is a competition: a probability of 0.350.35 is likely sufficient to win if the strongest rival has 0.10.1 probability. Standard training, however, treats 0.350.35 as high error and pushes the model toward p→1.0p\to 1.0. This trains the model to optimize overwhelming ("landslide") victories.

The broader theme is that standard training misallocates gradient pressure towards solutions that are already likely to be solved once the inference strategy is applied, without consideration of the utility of a single generation in context (Appendix F). To address this mismatch, we need to quantify the marginal utility of a sample to the TTS being used.

2.1 Test-Time Strategies as Differentiable Operators

Let 𝒳\mathcal{X} be the space of all possible inputs (prompts) and 𝒴\mathcal{Y} be the space of all possible generated sequences (solutions). For a given input x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}, the base policy πθ(⋅|x)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x) produces a probability distribution over the output space. We denote this distribution as residing in the standard probability simplex Δ|𝒴|−1\Delta^{|\mathcal{Y}|-1}.

For any TTS which takes as input a generative model and hyperparameters, we can represent it as a functional operator 𝒯:Δ|𝒴|−1×Φ→Δ|𝒴|−1\mathcal{T}:\Delta^{|\mathcal{Y}|-1}\times\Phi\rightarrow\Delta^{|\mathcal{Y}|-1}, mapping the base policy and hyperparameters ϕ∈Φ\phi\in\Phi (e.g., a sample budget N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N}) to an effective system-level policy π~θ\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}:

π~θ(y|x)=𝒯(πθ(⋅|x),ϕ)(y)\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(y|x)=\mathcal{T}(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x),\phi)(y) (1)

where y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y}. Sampling from this effective distribution demands greater test-time compute (e.g., a sampling budget of NN scales inference cost by a factor of NN relative to πθ\pi_{\theta}). As we will show, for many TTS, we can derive the functional form of 𝒯\mathcal{T}. Furthermore, that form is often differentiable with respect to the base policy probabilities πθ​(y′|x)\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}|x).

At deployment, predictions do not come from πθ\pi_{\theta} but from π~θ\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}. Thus, we want θ\theta such that π~θ\tilde{\pi}_{\theta} (not πθ\pi_{\theta}) is a Maximum Likelihood Estimator of the correct output y∗∈𝒴y^{*}\in\mathcal{Y} given xx. So, in the SFT setting, our goal is to minimize the induced loss over our training set 𝒟\mathcal{D}, defined as the negative log-likelihood of the ground truth output y∗y^{*} under the induced distribution:

ℒC​A​T​(θ)=−𝔼(x,y∗)∼𝒟​[log⁡π~θ​(y∗|x)]\mathcal{L}_{CAT}(\theta)=-\mathbb{E}_{(x,y^{*})\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[\log\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(y^{*}|x)\right] (2)

Let p=πθ​(y∗|x)∈[0,1]p=\pi_{\theta}(y^{*}|x)\in[0,1] denote the base probability of the correct answer, and p~=π~θ​(y∗|x)∈[0,1]\tilde{p}=\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(y^{*}|x)\in[0,1] denote the effective test-time probability. Differentiating the objective requires applying the chain rule over the entire output space 𝒴\mathcal{Y} (more details in Appendix A):

∇θℒC​A​T=−1p~∑y′∈𝒴∂p~∂πθ​(y′|x)∇θπθ(y′|x)\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{CAT}=-\frac{1}{\tilde{p}}\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}}\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}|x)}\nabla_{\theta}\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}|x) (3)

Importantly, we do not have the full vector πθ(⋅|x)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x), only pp. To avoid additional sampling, we need to approximate this gradient as a function of pp and ϕ\phi. Thus, we don’t compute this full Jacobian, as it requires evaluating the gradient through every possible alternative sequence y′y^{\prime}. We introduce a diagonal approximation of the Jacobian.

Theorem 1 (Diagonal Gradient Approximation).

Let the exact gradient of the CAT objective be decomposed into a diagonal term and an off-diagonal error vector:

ϵvec=∑y′≠y∗∂p~∂πθ​(y′|x)​∇θπθ​(y′|x)\epsilon_{\text{vec}}=\sum_{y^{\prime}\neq y^{*}}\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}|x)}\nabla_{\theta}\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}|x) (4)

Assuming the magnitude of the off-diagonal error ‖ϵvec‖\|\epsilon_{\text{vec}}\| is negligible relative to the diagonal gradient, the exact gradient can be approximated by scaling the standard Cross-Entropy SFT gradient (∇θℒC​E=−∇θ​log​p\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{CE}=-\nabla_{\theta}\log p) by a coefficient ww:

∇θℒC​A​T≈w⋅∇θℒC​Ewherew=pp~​∂p~∂p\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{CAT}\approx w\cdot\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{CE}\quad\text{where}\quad w=\frac{p}{\tilde{p}}\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p} (5)

p~\tilde{p}, and thus ww, may depend on the full probability vector beyond just the ground truth probability pp. However, if we can approximate p~\tilde{p} as a function of only pp and strategy hyperparameters ϕ\phi, the scaling coefficient simplifies to a tractable scalar function w⁡(p,ϕ)w(p,\phi).

The intuition is simple: often, the most important of the base probabilities πθ(⋅|x)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x) for selecting y∗y^{*} after search is the base probability of y∗y^{*}. We present sensitivity analysis for this approximation in Section A.8 and theoretical and empirical justification in all the cases we considered in Section A.9, Section A.11, Section B.3, and Section B.4. For an arbitrary search strategy, this is not guaranteed to be a good approximation; however, it allows us to use no additional compute to perform CAT.

This theorem provides our unified mechanism: the strategy communicates its requirements to the model by re-weighting the standard gradient based on the marginal test-time utility of the sample. By solving for p~\tilde{p}, specific scaling factors become corollaries of this theorem.

Corollary 1 (Pass@N Scaling Factor).

For Pass@N, success requires generating the correct answer at least once in NN attempts: p~=1−(1−p)N\tilde{p}=1-(1-p)^{N}. Because Pass@N success is invariant to the distribution of incorrect answers, ϵ=0\epsilon=0 and ∂p~∂p\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p} only depends on pp and NN, so the factor is exact. The SFT scaling factor is:

wp​a​s​s,S​F​T​(p,N)=N​p​(1−p)N−11−(1−p)Nw_{pass,SFT}(p,N)=\frac{Np(1-p)^{N-1}}{1-(1-p)^{N}} (6)
Corollary 2 (Majority Vote Scaling Factor).

For Majority Vote, success requires the correct answer to achieve plurality. To make this a function of pp and ϕ\phi, we approximate this as reaching a fixed consensus threshold kk within NN attempts yields p~=∑i=kN(Ni)​pi​(1−p)N−i\tilde{p}=\sum_{i=k}^{N}\binom{N}{i}p^{i}(1-p)^{N-i}. By setting kk to a fixed hyperparameter, ∂p~∂p\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p} is a function of pp and ϕ\phi. In Majority Vote, the true k is a function of terms in πθ​(⋅,x)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot,x) other than p. Thus, off-diagonal terms exist, but the diagonal approximation is safely bounded (see Section A.9). The SFT scaling factor is:

wm​a​j,S​F​T​(p,N,k)=k​(Nk)​pk​(1−p)N−k∑i=kN(Ni)​pi​(1−p)N−iw_{maj,SFT}(p,N,k)=\frac{k\binom{N}{k}p^{k}(1-p)^{N-k}}{\sum_{i=k}^{N}\binom{N}{i}p^{i}(1-p)^{N-i}} (7)

A similar derivation (Appendix B) shows that for RL, we reweigh gradients by a similar factor:

w⁡(p,ϕ)=∂p~∂pw(p,\phi)=\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p}

An intuition for why this is different than the SFT formulation is that RL optimizes utility, which is linear with respect to the policy, while SFT optimizes log probability, so the gradient passes through a log term. RL has the key distinction that we can use the empirical distribution from rollouts to dynamically estimate strategy parameters, such as the kk in Majority Vote, from the batch.

Corollary 3 (Best-of-NN Scaling Factor for RL).

For Best-of-NN in Reinforcement Learning, the strategy selects the candidate with the maximum reward from a batch of NN samples. Let P<yP_{<y} denote the probability of generating an output with a reward strictly less than R⁡(y|x)R(y|x). The effective probability that candidate yy wins the selection is π~θ​(y|x)=(P<y+πθ​(y|x))N−(P<y)N\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(y|x)=(P_{<y}+\pi_{\theta}(y|x))^{N}-(P_{<y})^{N}. Invoking the diagonal assumption with justification in Section B.3, ∂p~∂p=N​(P<y)N−1\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p}=N(P_{<y})^{N-1}. Since the RL scaling factor is this derivative, the weight is:

wb​o​n,R​L(πθ(⋅|x),N)=N(P<y)N−1w_{bon,RL}(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x),N)=N(P_{<y})^{N-1}

We can estimate P<yP_{<y} from the RL rollout batch via the empirical quantile P<y^\hat{P_{<y}}.

A table of weighing factors for common strategies can be seen in Table 1.

2.2 Interpreting the Scaling Factors

w⁡(p,ϕ)w(p,\phi) determines how strongly a sample influences training, based on its marginal contribution to test-time success. Gradients are amplified when a change meaningfully affects the final outcome, and suppressed when more confidence is redundant. Visualizations of each ww are in Appendix E.

Pass@NN

For Pass@N, ww decreases monotonically with the base probability pp. Once the model is likely to solve a problem within NN attempts, further increasing pp yields negligible improvement in Pass@NN performance. ww suppresses gradients on “easy” examples, allocating gradients only towards hard problems where marginal gains still improve coverage.

Majority Vote

Majority Vote success depends on surpassing competing answers. Accordingly, the scaling factor concentrates gradient mass near the consensus boundary. Samples that are already likely to win a plurality receive little to no signal.

Best-of-N

In Best-of-N RL, the scaling factor depends on a sample’s rank within the reward distribution rather than its absolute likelihood. This induces winner-take-all dynamics: gradients reinforce the highest-reward samples, while lower-reward outputs are ignored.

3 Experiments

To empirically validate CAT, we show how it extends Chen et al. [8] by evaluating the method on three progressive axes to demonstrate its generality: moving beyond Pass@NN to majority vote, beyond SFT to Reinforcement Learning, and beyond LLMs to PLMs.

For our language modeling experiments, we fine-tune the Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 model [13] on the MATH benchmark [14]. To isolate the effect of strategy-aware loss from general feature learning and save compute, all models first undergo a shared two-epoch "warmup" phase using standard cross-entropy. This stabilizes the base policy πθ\pi_{\theta} into a regime of non-trivial success probability, which helps to ensure the strategy-aware gradient scaling factors w⁡(p,ϕ)w(p,\phi) remain numerically stable (see Section A.6) before branching into the experimental CAT regimes.

3.1 Beyond Pass@NN: Maj Vote in SFT

Prior work has demonstrated that standard cross-entropy is misaligned with Pass@NN [8]. We first validate our CAT framework by recovering this result. As shown in Table 2 and Figure 1, applying the Pass@NN CAT objective actively suppresses overconfidence on easy samples. Models trained with larger budgets (e.g., N=64N=64) incur a "tax" on single-sample accuracy (Pass@1 drops by 2.28%) but yield a 7.80% absolute improvement in Pass@64 coverage over the SFT baseline.

To validate CAT more broadly, we transition to Majority Vote. We trained models across varying budgets N∈{8,16,64}N\in\{8,16,64\} selecting kk for each model via sweeps (Section I.4). In the previous experiment, we trained the models on just answers, whereas in this experiment, we used both answers and solution traces. Our rationale is that Majority Vote relies on CoT while Pass@N does not.

As detailed in Table 3 and Figure 2, CAT strictly outperforms the baseline when Majority Vote is applied. Interestingly, we observe a "sweet spot" at N=16N=16 where this model broadly outperforms all the others. This highlights a bias-variance tradeoff inherent to CAT (characterized theoretically in Section A.6). For some strategies, gradient variance increases as intended compute budget increases. Furthermore, the choice of hyperparameter kk may have been more accurate for N=16N=16 than the other strategies. Regardless, all models show improved performance when the TTS is applied.

3.2 Beyond SFT: Reinforcement Learning

Having established CAT’s efficacy for SFT, we extend the framework to RL. To algin RL, we modify the GRPO objective by applying our scaling factors directly to the normalized advantages (derivation in Appendix C). We evaluate the CAT models on both Pass@NN and Majority Vote, utilizing the MATH benchmark. The models undergo a brief SFT warmup before transitioning to one epoch of strategy-aligned GRPO.

Pass@NN Coverage Validation.

As shown in Figure 4 and Table 5, standard RL exhibits poor test-time scaling. While it achieves a respectable Pass@1 (8.27%), its performance saturates quickly due to policy collapse, reaching only 35.80% at k=32k=32. In contrast, our CAT models explicitly preserve the variance necessary for test-time discovery. The Pass@16 model reaches 40.00% at k=32k=32, a substantial relative improvement over the baseline. Furthermore, the Pass@4 model improved Pass@1 coverage over the base model. The reason for this is how CAT interacts with the RL generation process. We offer a deeper explanation for this and how CAT can be used to improve Pass@1 coverage in Appendix D.

Majority Vote Consensus Validation.

A fundamental difference between RL and SFT CAT for Majority Vote is that the rollouts in RL allow us to estimate the threshold kk from the rollout batch, while SFT forces us to set that as a hyperparameter. As detailed in Figure 4 and Table 5, Standard RL scales suboptimally under Majority Vote aggregation. Conversely, the CAT-trained models trade off a marginal amount of Pass@1 accuracy to successfully shape the distribution for consensus.

3.3 Beyond LLMs: Best-of-NN in Protein Generation

To demonstrate that our framework is modality-agnostic, we investigate Best-of-NN (BoN) RL using Protein Language Models (PLMs). Standard RL optimizes the expected reward, making it inherently risk-averse. Conversely, BoN RL optimizes the maximum reward of a batch, acting as a filter. The objective signals that generating failures is permissible, provided the variance is high enough to produce a single high-reward output. A qualitative difference between BoN and the other strategies is that BoN has no single best answer. As such, we have to estimate the quantile of a given answer within the rollout batch Section B.2.3. We test CAT in two settings using the ProtGPT2 [15] model.

Experiment 1: The "Valley of Death".

We defined the reward R⁡(x)R(x) as a function of protein hydrophobicity h⁡(x)h(x) (see Appendix M for the details). In protein engineering, hydrophobicity is often a useful property in designing stable transmembrane domains. From an optimization perspective, this can create non-convex rewards. In these scenarios, materials with low-hydrophobicity create safe water-soluble structures, medium-hydrophobicity structures tend to misfold, and high-hydrophobicity structures are the most stable [16, 17]. The resulting landscape a multi-modal containing a local hydrophilic maximum (h≈0.35h\approx 0.35), a heavily penalized aggregation zone (h≈0.50h\approx 0.50), and a narrow global maximum (h≈0.75h\approx 0.75). As shown in Figure 6 (Left), Standard RL converges into the local maximum, while BoN-trained models (N∈{2,4,8}N\in\{2,4,8\}) bifurcate their distributions, sacrificing average reward to reach the global maximum.

Experiment 2: Complementary Hydrophobicity.

In therapeutic and biomaterials design, practitioners frequently need to generate complementary sequences, such as solubility tags, that perfectly counterbalance the properties of a target protein to maintain stability [18, 19]. As such, we evaluated the framework on a task requiring the model to generate a sequence with inverse hydrophobicity to an input (ht​a​r​g​e​t=1.0−hi​nh_{target}=1.0-h_{in}). Standard RL clusters around a narrow, safe mean, failing to capture the full relational range. Figure 6 (Right) shows that BoN training induces a "stretching" effect. The model learns to output a wider variance of candidates, increasing the probability that at least one sample will perfectly complement the input target.

Results.

Table 6, Figure 8, and Figure 8 detail the expected maximum reward at varying test-time budgets. In both settings, Standard RL underperforms under test time scaling because its narrow distribution lacks the diversity required for a search process. The most informative result is in the more complex second experiment. While BoN-trained models pay a "Search Tax" (lower single-sample quality at N=1N=1), they exhibit superior scaling curves, saturating near the theoretical maximums when allowed to search.

4 Discussion

By formalizing inference as an operator, we show that training should be aligned with the distribution induced by the test-time procedure rather than the base policy. This addresses a fundamental mismatch in modern generative modeling: while deployment generates multiple outputs, standard objectives optimize single-output performance. CAT provides a simple and efficient mechanism to correct this mismatch without increasing training cost. Across SFT and RL, we observe that alignment with test-time strategies consistently improves scaling with inference compute. Furthermore, results on protein generation demonstrate that this principle extends beyond language models. Together, these findings suggest that training objectives should be designed with the downstream inference procedure in mind, especially as test-time compute becomes increasingly central to enhancing model capability. Conceptualizing inference as an operator provides a principled mechanism to achieve this goal.

Limitations

While CAT provides a theoretically sound bridge between training and deployment, it introduces specific optimization challenges. First, as analyzed in our variance analysis (Section A.6 and Section B.6), strategy-aware gradients can exhibit severe variance inflation, which can degrade performance. Developing principled variance reduction techniques for these objectives is a promising direction for future work. Second, our framework relies on the diagonal approximation of the effective test-time probability. While we show this approximation is well-justified in the settings we consider (Section A.9), it may underestimate the full learning signal. Extending the framework to account for cross-output dependencies, or understanding the benefits of allocating additional compute to approximate the full gradient, remains an important avenue for further study. More broadly, we have focused on a set of relatively simple test-time strategies. A natural extension is to apply this operator-based alignment to more complex, multi-step search algorithms, such as Genetic Algorithms [20] or Monte Carlo Tree Search [21], where π~θ\tilde{\pi}_{\theta} may not admit a simple functional dependence on πθ\pi_{\theta} and ϕ\phi or more complex agentic settings [22] which functional forms may be impossible to derive whatsoever. Finally, understanding how CAT affects the underlying generation process during RL (Appendix D) presents an additional direction for future work.

Appendix A Derivations and Explanations for SFT

This section adds detail to the derivations for the SFT CAT losses, as well as some additional useful theoretical results about these factors, including an analysis of the accuracy of the diagonal approximation. We generally presume SFT aims to minimize standard Cross-Entropy loss (ℒCE\mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}), defined as the negative log-likelihood of the ground truth labels under the base policy:

ℒCE​(θ)=−𝔼(x,y)∼𝒟​[log⁡πθ​(y∣x)]\mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}(\theta)=-\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[\log\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)\right] (8)

We define a Test-Time Strategy (TTS) as a functional operator 𝒯\mathcal{T} applied to the base policy πθ\pi_{\theta}. Let π~θ​(y∣x)=𝒯⁡(πθ,ϕ)​(y∣x)\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(y\mid x)=\mathcal{T}(\pi_{\theta},\phi)(y\mid x) denote the system-level probability that the generative model ultimately yields the target output yy given the input xx after the TTS is applied. The term ϕ\phi represents the hyperparameters of the strategy, such as the sample budget NN in Pass@NN.

We define the Compute Aligned Training (CAT) loss (ℒCAT\mathcal{L}_{\text{CAT}}) as the negative log-likelihood of the ground truth data under this effective system-level policy:

ℒCAT​(θ)=−𝔼(x,y)∼𝒟​[log⁡π~θ​(y∣x)]=−𝔼(x,y)∼𝒟​[log⁡(𝒯⁡(πθ,ϕ)​(y∣x))]\lx@nobreakspace\lx@nobreakspace\mathcal{L}_{\text{CAT}}(\theta)=-\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[\log\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(y\mid x)\right]=-\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[\log\left(\mathcal{T}(\pi_{\theta},\phi)(y\mid x)\right)\right] (9)

Note that a very similar setup would work for loss functions other than cross-entropy, but we limit our scope to cross-entropy for simplicity.

A.1 Gradient of ℒCAT\mathcal{L}_{\text{CAT}}

We derive the gradient of the new objective ℒCAT\mathcal{L}_{\text{CAT}} with respect to the model parameters θ\theta.

Let p~=π~θ​(y∗∣x)\tilde{p}=\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(y^{*}\mid x) denote the probability of success (generating the ground truth y∗y^{*}) under the test-time strategy. p~\tilde{p} is a function of the entire policy vector πθ(⋅∣x)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x).

Applying the chain rule over the output space 𝒴\mathcal{Y}:

∇θℒCAT\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\text{CAT}} =−∇θ​log​p~\displaystyle=-\nabla_{\theta}\log\tilde{p}
=−1p~​∇θ​p~\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{\tilde{p}}\nabla_{\theta}\tilde{p}
=−1p~∑y′∈𝒴∂p~∂πθ​(y′∣x)∇θπθ(y′∣x)\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{\tilde{p}}\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}}\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}\nabla_{\theta}\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}\mid x) (10)

The above equation presents a practical challenge. In the standard SFT regime, we efficiently compute πθ​(y∗∣x)\pi_{\theta}(y^{*}\mid x) (the ground truth probability), but we do not have access to the probabilities of arbitrary alternative outputs πθ​(y′∣x)\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}\mid x) without sampling.

We briefly touch on ways to incorporate some of these missing diagonal elements in Section A.7. However, we assume that the majority of the change in probability of success is accounted for by the change in the probability of outputting the correct answer. Theoretical justification is given in Section A.8. Furthermore, take p~\tilde{p} to be well-approximated as a function of p=πθ​(y∗∣x)p=\pi_{\theta}(y^{*}\mid x) and the sum to be 00 for terms where y′≠y∗y^{\prime}\neq y^{*}.

Applying these assumptions, we get:

∇θℒCAT\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\text{CAT}} ≈−1p~​∂p~∂p​∇θp\displaystyle\approx-\frac{1}{\tilde{p}}\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p}\nabla_{\theta}p
=−pp~​∂p~∂p​∇θl​o​g​(p)\displaystyle=-\frac{p}{\tilde{p}}\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p}\nabla_{\theta}log(p)
=(pp~​∂p~∂p)⏟w⁡(p,ϕ)⋅∇θℒCE\displaystyle=\underbrace{\left(\frac{p}{\tilde{p}}\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p}\right)}_{w(p,\phi)}\cdot\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}} (11)

The Test-Time Aware update is simply the standard gradient scaled by a scalar coefficient w⁡(p,ϕ)w(p,\phi), keeping the computational cost of training comparable to standard SFT.

A.2 Deriving ww for Pass@NN

It is worth noting that this instance of CAT is Direct Coverage Optimization from Chen et al. [8]. We credit their ideas for inspiring this work.

The hyperparameter ϕ\phi is the sample budget NN. Pass@NN samples NN independent solutions from the base model πθ\pi_{\theta}. The strategy is successful if at least one of the NN samples is correct.

Let p=πθ​(y∗∣x)p=\pi_{\theta}(y^{*}\mid x) be the probability that a single sample is correct (i.e., Pass@1). The probability of generating an incorrect answer is 1−p1-p. The probability that all NN samples fail is (1−p)N(1-p)^{N}. Therefore, the effective probability of success, p~\tilde{p}, is:

p~=1−(1−p)N\tilde{p}=1-(1-p)^{N} (12)

We first compute the partial derivative of p~\tilde{p} with respect to the base probability pp:

∂p~∂p=∂∂p​[1−(1−p)N]=−(N​(1−p)N−1⋅(−1))=N​(1−p)N−1\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p}=\frac{\partial}{\partial p}\left[1-(1-p)^{N}\right]=-\left(N(1-p)^{N-1}\cdot(-1)\right)=N(1-p)^{N-1} (13)

Recall the definition of the scaling factor derived in Section A.1:

w⁡(p,N)=pp~​∂p~∂pw(p,N)=\frac{p}{\tilde{p}}\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p}

Substituting our expressions for p~\tilde{p} and ∂p~∂p\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p}, we obtain the closed-form scaling coefficient for Pass@NN:

w⁡(p,N)\displaystyle w(p,N) =p1−(1−p)N⋅N​(1−p)N−1\displaystyle=\frac{p}{1-(1-p)^{N}}\cdot N(1-p)^{N-1}
=N​p​(1−p)N−11−(1−p)N\displaystyle=\frac{Np(1-p)^{N-1}}{1-(1-p)^{N}} (14)

For the trivial case where N=1N=1, the term simplifies to w⁡(p,1)=1w(p,1)=1, recovering the standard cross-entropy objective.

The behavior of the scaling factor wpassw_{\text{pass}} provides intuitive insight into why this objective prevents model overconfidence. It is monotonically decreasing as p→1p\rightarrow 1.

Intuition: The Pass@NN objective acts as a natural regularizer. It signals to the optimizer: "The model is already likely enough to generate the correct answer within NN tries; stop updating parameters for this sample and focus on harder examples." This prevents the model from wasting capacity on memorizing "easy" prompts. A more thorough discussion of the meaning of this weighing factor can be found in [8].

A.3 Majority Vote in SFT

Coming from the work of Wang et al. [6], Majority Vote is a plurality vote: the correct answer y∗y^{*} is selected if it appears more frequently than any specific incorrect answer y′y^{\prime}. Thus p~\tilde{p} clearly depends on more than just pp but on the full distribution of πθ(⋅|x)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x). To render this tractable and dependent solely on the scalar pp, we approximate the strategy using a fixed threshold relaxation.

We define success as the correct answer appearing at least kk times in NN samples. In truth, this kk is a function of the distribution of incorrect answers. By setting a fixed threshold, so long as a single incorrect answer doesn’t appear more than kk times out of NN draws, this objective will cause the majority vote to get the right answer with less overconfidence than what SFT would give it. k=⌊N/2⌋+1k=\lfloor N/2\rfloor+1 serves as a strict upper bound on kk on what this threshold could be, so it serves as a worst case for what we should set kk to. The count of correct answers follows a Binomial distribution ny∗∼Bin​(N,p)n_{y^{*}}\sim\text{Bin}(N,p). The effective probability is the regularized incomplete beta function:

p~maj=Pr⁡(ny∗≥k)=∑i=kN(Ni)​pi​(1−p)N−i\tilde{p}_{\text{maj}}=\Pr(n_{y^{*}}\geq k)=\sum_{i=k}^{N}\binom{N}{i}p^{i}(1-p)^{N-i} (15)

The derivative of this cumulative sum with respect to pp is proportional to the probability mass at the decision boundary kk. The scaling factor becomes:

wmaj​(p,N,k)=k​(Nk)​pk​(1−p)N−k∑i=kN(Ni)​pi​(1−p)N−iw_{\text{maj}}(p,N,k)=\frac{k\binom{N}{k}p^{k}(1-p)^{N-k}}{\sum_{i=k}^{N}\binom{N}{i}p^{i}(1-p)^{N-i}} (16)
Interpretation:

The numerator represents the probability of being exactly at the threshold of consensus (having kk correct answers). The denominator is the total probability of having achieved consensus.

  • •

    If the model is far from consensus (p≪k/Np\ll k/N), the gradient is boosted effectively to push the mass over the decision boundary.

  • •

    If the model has achieved stable consensus (p≫k/Np\gg k/N), the denominator approaches 1 and the numerator approaches 0, annealing the gradient to preserve the solution.

A.4 Best-of-NN SFT

In an SFT setting with nonbinary scores, there’s many ways data can be presented to use. In the setting where we are always given a ground truth best possible answer, the problem reduces to Pass@NN, so we do not provide any experiments or derivations for this. The scope of this paper will not go into all of the different ways nonbinary reward data can be presented for fine tuning.

A.5 Reasoning Traces and Data Constraints

The derivations in the prior subsections operate under the simplified assumption that πθ​(y∣x)\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x) represents the probability of generating the correct final answer yy. However, in modern reasoning models utilizing COT, the generation process is more complex. The model produces a reasoning trace zz (a sequence of intermediate tokens) followed by a final answer yy.

Formally, the probability of generating a specific answer yy is the marginal probability over all possible latent reasoning paths 𝒵\mathcal{Z}:

πθ​(y∣x)=∑z∈𝒵πθ​(y,z∣x)=∑z∈𝒵πθ​(y∣z,x)​πθ​(z∣x)\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)=\sum_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}\pi_{\theta}(y,z\mid x)=\sum_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}\pi_{\theta}(y\mid z,x)\pi_{\theta}(z\mid x) (17)

Test-time strategies like Majority Vote or Pass@N are concerned exclusively with this marginal probability πθ​(y∣x)\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x). We care whether the final answer is correct, regardless of the specific reasoning path taken.

This distinction introduces a practical difficulty for Supervised Fine-Tuning. In a standard SFT setting, our training dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D} typically consists of triplets (x,z∗,y∗)(x,z^{*},y^{*}), where z∗z^{*} is a single "golden" reasoning trace provided by human annotators or synthetic data generation.

We do not have access to the full marginal distribution πθ​(y∗∣x)\pi_{\theta}(y^{*}\mid x) during training, as marginalizing over the exponentially large space of all possible reasoning paths 𝒵\mathcal{Z} is computationally intractable. Instead, since πθ​(y∗,z∗∣x)≤πθ​(y∗∣x)\pi_{\theta}(y^{*},z^{*}\mid x)\leq\pi_{\theta}(y^{*}\mid x), the likelihood of the provided trace serves as a tractable lower bound for the true marginal probability. In practice, we use this single-trace likelihood as a direct proxy for pp when computing the scaling factor w⁡(p,ϕ)w(p,\phi). This approximation allows us to apply test-time aligned gradient scaling efficiently without the need for expensive sampling or marginalization over the latent space. This can be interpreted as training the model for the specific reasoning trace (z∗,y∗)(z^{*},y^{*}) to be selected as the TTS. This is what is done for standard SFT under Pass@11 and it works empirically, so we stick to this formulation to avoid sampling.

Furthermore, in practice, we begin by warming up the model on classic SFT. This is useful because it teaches the model to associate the provided reasoning trace z∗z^{*} with the correct answer y∗y^{*} before strategy-aware modulation takes over. In the low-probability regime (p→0p\to 0), the scaling factors typically a constant (e.g., w⁡(p)≈1w(p)\approx 1 for Pass@NN), rendering the CAT gradient directionally equivalent to the standard SFT gradient. Warmup leverages this alignment to ’ground’ the reasoning process, ensuring that subsequent strategy-aware updates optimize a policy that generates the answer via a valid chain of thought, rather than exploiting spurious correlations in the marginal distribution.

A.6 Variance Analysis: The Variance Inflation Factor

To quantify the stability of the CAT objective, we define the Variance Inflation (VI) factor. Because the strategy-aware SFT gradient is formulated as ∇θℒCAT=w⁡(p,ϕ)​∇θℒCE\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\text{CAT}}=w(p,\phi)\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}, we can cleanly isolate the impact of our objective on optimization stability. We measure this via the ratio of the squared gradient norms for a specific sample xx:

VI​(x)=∥∇θℒCAT∥2∥∇θℒCE∥2=|w⁡(p,ϕ)|2=|pp~​∂p~∂p|2\text{VI}(x)=\frac{\lVert\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\text{CAT}}\rVert^{2}}{\lVert\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}\rVert^{2}}=|w(p,\phi)|^{2}=\left|\frac{p}{\tilde{p}}\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p}\right|^{2} (18)

To identify potential stability risks, we focus our analysis on the asymptotic behavior of the VI for "hard" samples, taking the limit as the base probability approaches zero (p→0p\to 0). We examine this specific limit because as models master "easy" samples (p→1p\to 1), strategy-aware scaling factors naturally decay to zero (or remain strictly bounded), suppressing gradient variance. Optimization catastrophes in this framework almost exclusively originate from the aggressive up-weighting of highly uncertain predictions.

Pass@NN: Stability.

For Pass@NN, p~=1−(1−p)N\tilde{p}=1-(1-p)^{N}. The scaling factor is:

wpass​(p)=p⋅N​(1−p)N−11−(1−p)Nw_{\text{pass}}(p)=\frac{p\cdot N(1-p)^{N-1}}{1-(1-p)^{N}} (19)

Analyzing the limit as p→0p\to 0 using the first-order Taylor expansion (1−p)N≈1−N​p(1-p)^{N}\approx 1-Np:

limp→0Fpass​(p)≈p⋅N⁡(1)1−(1−N​p)=N​pN​p=1\lim_{p\to 0}F_{\text{pass}}(p)\approx\frac{p\cdot N(1)}{1-(1-Np)}=\frac{Np}{Np}=1 (20)

Conclusion: Pass@NN SFT is inherently stable. The VI approaches 1 for hard samples and decays to 0 for easy samples. It does not introduce variance explosion.

Majority Vote: Instability.

For Majority Vote, we approximate the success probability near p→0p\to 0 using the leading term of the Binomial sum (where k≈N/2k\approx N/2 is the threshold):

p~≈(Nk)​pk​(1−p)N−k⟹∂p~∂p≈k​(Nk)​pk−1\tilde{p}\approx\binom{N}{k}p^{k}(1-p)^{N-k}\implies\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p}\approx k\binom{N}{k}p^{k-1} (21)

Substituting this into the definition of ww:

limp→0wmaj​(p)=p(Nk)​pk⋅k​(Nk)​pk−1=p⋅k⋅pk−1pk=k\lim_{p\to 0}w_{\text{maj}}(p)=\frac{p}{\binom{N}{k}p^{k}}\cdot k\binom{N}{k}p^{k-1}=\frac{p\cdot k\cdot p^{k-1}}{p^{k}}=k (22)

Conclusion: For Majority Vote, the gradient for hard samples is boosted by a factor of k≈N/2k\approx N/2. The variance scales quadratically:

VImaj≈(N2)2=N24\text{VI}_{\text{maj}}\approx\left(\frac{N}{2}\right)^{2}=\frac{N^{2}}{4} (23)

This theoretical bound confirms that Majority Vote SFT is highly prone to variance explosion for hard examples as NN increases.

A.7 Beyond the Diagonal Assumption: Token-Level Dependencies

The derivation of w⁡(p,ϕ)w(p,\phi) in the previous sections relies on the simplifying assumption that the effective test-time probability p~\tilde{p} is a function of the ground truth probability p=πθ​(y∗|x)p=\pi_{\theta}(y^{*}|x), instead of all of πθ(⋅|x)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x). While this holds for Pass@NN, it is an approximation for Majority Vote.

In a Majority Vote setting, the probability of the correct answer y∗y^{*} achieving a consensus depends not just on its own likelihood, but on the distribution of the incorrect mass. A scenario where the remaining probability mass 1−p1-p is concentrated on a single "strong rival" answer y′y^{\prime} is fundamentally different from a scenario where it is dispersed uniformly over the vocabulary. To address this without the computational cost of full Monte Carlo resampling during training, we propose examining the logits at the token level.

A.7.1 The Greedy Bound via Token Margins

We posit that the strength of the "rival" consensus can be bounded by analyzing the decision margin at each generation step. Let y∗=(y1∗,…,yT∗)y^{*}=(y^{*}_{1},\dots,y^{*}_{T}) be the ground truth sequence. At any timestep tt, let zt∈ℝ|V|z_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{|V|} denote the logits where VV is the vocabulary. We define the token margin δt\delta_{t} as the distance between the logit of the correct token and the most likely incorrect token (the "greedy rival"):

δt=zt​[yt∗]−maxv≠yt∗⁡zt​[v]\delta_{t}=z_{t}[y^{*}_{t}]-\max_{v\neq y^{*}_{t}}z_{t}[v] (24)

This margin acts as a proxy for the local stability of the generation. A large positive δt\delta_{t} implies that the model is locally robust against deviating to an alternative path. Conversely, a small or negative δt\delta_{t} identifies a "weak link" where a rival answer could plausibly capture the search process.

We can approximate the probability ratio between the ground truth y∗y^{*} and the most likely rival sequence y′y^{\prime} via the minimum margin over the sequence:

P⁡(y′)P⁡(y∗)≈exp⁡(−mint⁡δt)\frac{P(y^{\prime})}{P(y^{*})}\approx\exp\left(-\min_{t}\delta_{t}\right) (25)

This formulation allows us to estimate parameters such as the effective consensus difficulty without explicit sampling. For example, if the minimum margin is small, the rival is strong, implying that a higher effective count kk is required to ensure y∗y^{*} dominates the vote.

A.7.2 Contrastive Margin Maximization

To directly suppress the probability of the rival answer y′y^{\prime}, we introduce a contrastive auxiliary loss. Rather than simply maximizing the likelihood of y∗y^{*} (which can be satisfied even if a rival y′y^{\prime} is also highly likely), we explicitly maximize the gap between the truth and the nearest incorrect trajectory.

We define the Contrastive Majority Loss as:

ℒContrast=1T​∑t=1Tmax⁡(0,η−δt)\mathcal{L}_{\text{Contrast}}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\max(0,\eta-\delta_{t}) (26)

where η\eta is a target margin hyperparameter. By minimizing this objective, we force the model to not only generate the correct answer but to do so with sufficient distance from the "second-best" hypothesis. This effectively "clears the field" for the Majority Vote operator, ensuring that p⁡(y∗)p(y^{*}) is dominant relative to the most probable incorrect aggregate maxy≠y∗⁡p⁡(y)\max_{y\neq y^{*}}p(y).

This is just a heuristic meant to show that a user can consider the full distribution, but practically we still recommend the strategy used in Appendix I.

A.7.3 Empirical Validation of Token-Level Margins

To validate the theoretical benefit of addressing token-level dependencies and suppressing rival probability mass, we conducted a preliminary, small-scale proof-of-concept experiment on a subset of the MATH benchmark. We compared a standard SFT baseline against both our standard CAT Majority Vote implementation and a hybrid objective that incorporates Contrastive Margin Maximization.

Experimental Setup

We utilized the 4-bit quantized Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 model. To ensure a stable initialization and isolate the effect of the strategy-aware losses, all models underwent a shared warmup phase consisting of one epoch of standard cross-entropy training. Following warmup, the training branched into three distinct one-epoch regimes:

  1. 1.

    SFT Baseline: Continued standard cross-entropy training.

  2. 2.

    CAT Majority Vote: Training using the CAT objective.

  3. 3.

    Pairwise Contrastive (Hybrid): A joint objective combining standard SFT with a token-level contrastive loss, weighted equally (0.5⋅ℒCE+0.5⋅ℒContrast0.5\cdot\mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}+0.5\cdot\mathcal{L}_{\text{Contrast}}).

Contrastive Implementation

Instead of explicitly calculating the full margin over the sequence, we implemented a computationally efficient pairwise approximation. For each valid token in the ground truth sequence, we sampled M=4M=4 alternative "rival" tokens from the model’s current probability distribution (masking out the ground truth). Let z∗z^{*} be the logit of the correct token, and zbadz_{\text{bad}} be the logit of a sampled rival. The contrastive loss maximizes the difference between these logits using a log-sigmoid function:

ℒContrast=−1M∑i=1Mlogσ(z∗−zbad(i))\mathcal{L}_{\text{Contrast}}=-\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}\log\sigma\left(z^{*}-z_{\text{bad}}^{(i)}\right) (27)

This objective explicitly pushes down the probability mass of the most likely incorrect paths, "clearing the field" to ensure the ground truth answer dominates the inference-time voting process.

Results and Discussion

We evaluated the models by generating N=64N=64 candidate solutions per problem. The results are summarized in Table 7.

The results align well with our theoretical framework. The CAT Majority Vote model successfully improves both single-sample precision (13.03%13.03\%) and overall consensus performance (17.60%17.60\%) compared to the standard SFT baseline.

Crucially, the Pairwise Contrastive model highlights the specific dynamics of test-time search. It experiences a minor degradation in single-sample precision compared to the baseline (Pass@1 drops to 12.47%12.47\%), demonstrating the "search tax" where optimizing for aggregation slightly degrades the mean trajectory. However, this tradeoff yields a distribution far better suited for aggregation. It achieves the highest absolute Majority Vote accuracy (18.20%18.20\%), and its "Aggregation Gain" (the absolute performance delta between Pass@1 and Majority Vote) nearly doubles the baseline, reaching 5.72%5.72\%.

While this remains a limited-scale proof of concept, it successfully supports the hypothesis that standard cross-entropy leaves test-time performance on the table by ignoring the distribution of incorrect answers. Actively penalizing strong rival tokens ensures that when the model generates the correct reasoning trace, it does so with enough local stability to win a plurality vote.

A.8 Sensitivity Analysis of the Diagonal Approximation

In Section 2.1, we introduced the diagonal approximation to avoid the computational intractability of evaluating the full Jacobian over the entire output space 𝒴\mathcal{Y}. The previous subsection described a heuristic used to compensate the approximation. Here, we formally study the error introduced by this approximation.

Let the exact gradient of our objective be gexact=∇θℒC​A​Tg_{\text{exact}}=\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{CAT}, and our diagonal approximation be gdiag=w⁡(p,ϕ)​∇θℒC​Eg_{\text{diag}}=w(p,\phi)\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{CE}. The exact gradient can be decomposed into the diagonal term and an off-diagonal error vector ϵvec\epsilon_{\text{vec}}:

gexact=gdiag+ϵvecwhereϵvec=−1p~∑y′∈ℛ∂p~∂πθ​(y′|x)∇θπθ(y′|x)g_{\text{exact}}=g_{\text{diag}}+\epsilon_{\text{vec}}\quad\text{where}\quad\epsilon_{\text{vec}}=-\frac{1}{\tilde{p}}\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}}\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}|x)}\nabla_{\theta}\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}|x) (28)

where ℛ={y′∈𝒴∣y′≠y∗}\mathcal{R}=\{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}\mid y^{\prime}\neq y^{*}\} is the set of incorrect (rival) sequences.

To determine how optimizing with our diagonal approximation gdiagg_{\text{diag}} affects the true objective ℒC​A​T\mathcal{L}_{CAT}, we must analyze the objective’s behavior under a standard gradient descent update. Let the model parameters at step tt be updated using the approximate gradient with a sufficiently small learning rate η>0\eta>0, such that θt+1=θt−η​gdiag\theta_{t+1}=\theta_{t}-\eta g_{\text{diag}}.

Assuming ℒC​A​T\mathcal{L}_{CAT} is locally differentiable, we can apply a first-order Taylor expansion to evaluate the resulting change in the exact loss:

ℒC​A​T​(θt+1)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{CAT}(\theta_{t+1}) ≈ℒC​A​T​(θt)+∇θℒC​A​T​(θt)T​(θt+1−θt)\displaystyle\approx\mathcal{L}_{CAT}(\theta_{t})+\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{CAT}(\theta_{t})^{T}(\theta_{t+1}-\theta_{t})
ℒC​A​T​(θt+1)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{CAT}(\theta_{t+1}) ≈ℒC​A​T​(θt)−η⁡⟨gexact,gdiag⟩\displaystyle\approx\mathcal{L}_{CAT}(\theta_{t})-\eta\langle g_{\text{exact}},g_{\text{diag}}\rangle (29)

We must first validate that this update is directionally aligned with our goal. For the parameter update to yield a strict decrease in the true objective (ℒC​A​T​(θt+1)<ℒC​A​T​(θt)\mathcal{L}_{CAT}(\theta_{t+1})<\mathcal{L}_{CAT}(\theta_{t})), the inner product ⟨gexact,gdiag⟩\langle g_{\text{exact}},g_{\text{diag}}\rangle must be strictly positive.

Theorem 2 (Approximation Descent Condition).

The diagonal approximation gdiagg_{\text{diag}} guarantees a strict decrease in the exact loss ℒC​A​T\mathcal{L}_{CAT} if the magnitude of the off-diagonal error vector is strictly bounded by the magnitude of the diagonal gradient: ‖ϵvec‖<‖gdiag‖\|\epsilon_{\text{vec}}\|<\|g_{\text{diag}}\|.

Proof. Expanding the inner product yields ⟨gdiag,gdiag+ϵvec⟩=‖gdiag‖2+⟨gdiag,ϵvec⟩\langle g_{\text{diag}},g_{\text{diag}}+\epsilon_{\text{vec}}\rangle=\|g_{\text{diag}}\|^{2}+\langle g_{\text{diag}},\epsilon_{\text{vec}}\rangle. By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, the worst-case adversarial perturbation occurs when ϵvec\epsilon_{\text{vec}} points in the exact opposite direction of gdiagg_{\text{diag}}. Setting ‖gdiag‖2−‖gdiag‖​‖ϵvec‖>0\|g_{\text{diag}}\|^{2}-\|g_{\text{diag}}\|\|\epsilon_{\text{vec}}\|>0 yields the strict descent bound ‖ϵvec‖<‖gdiag‖\|\epsilon_{\text{vec}}\|<\|g_{\text{diag}}\|.

While Theorem 2 establishes a worst-case bound for descent, we can derive a much stronger typical-case alignment by analyzing the structural properties of the inner product ⟨gdiag,ϵvec⟩\langle g_{\text{diag}},\epsilon_{\text{vec}}\rangle.

Let us expand the off-diagonal error vector using the log-derivative trick, ∇θπθ​(y′|x)=πθ​(y′|x)​∇θ​log⁡πθ​(y′|x)\nabla_{\theta}\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}|x)=\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}|x)\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}|x):

ϵvec=−1p~∑y′∈ℛ∂p~∂πθ​(y′|x)πθ(y′|x)∇θlogπθ(y′|x)\epsilon_{\text{vec}}=-\frac{1}{\tilde{p}}\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}}\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}|x)}\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}|x)\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}|x) (30)

Taking the inner product with the diagonal approximation gdiag=−w⁡(p,ϕ)​∇θ​log⁡πθ​(y∗|x)g_{\text{diag}}=-w(p,\phi)\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y^{*}|x) yields:

⟨gdiag,ϵvec⟩=w⁡(p,ϕ)p~​∑y′∈ℛπθ​(y′|x)​∂p~∂πθ​(y′|x)​𝒞θ​(y∗,y′)\langle g_{\text{diag}},\epsilon_{\text{vec}}\rangle=\frac{w(p,\phi)}{\tilde{p}}\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}}\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}|x)\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}|x)}\mathcal{C}_{\theta}(y^{*},y^{\prime}) (31)

where 𝒞θ​(y∗,y′)=⟨∇θ​log​πθ​(y∗|x),∇θ​log​πθ​(y′|x)⟩\mathcal{C}_{\theta}(y^{*},y^{\prime})=\langle\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y^{*}|x),\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}|x)\rangle.

To evaluate this inner product, we introduce the Proportional Decay Assumption. In any model with a softmax output, an increase in the ground truth probability p=πθ​(y∗|x)p=\pi_{\theta}(y^{*}|x) draws mass from rival tokens proportional to their current probability [23]. Therefore, the gradient of a rival can be approximated as:

∇θπθ​(y′|x)≈−πθ​(y′|x)1−p​∇θp\nabla_{\theta}\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}|x)\approx-\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}|x)}{1-p}\nabla_{\theta}p

Dividing by πθ​(y′|x)\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}|x) and applying the log-derivative trick, we establish a deterministic relationship between the log-gradients:

∇θ​log​πθ​(y′|x)≈−p1−p​∇θ​log​p\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}|x)\approx-\frac{p}{1-p}\nabla_{\theta}\log p

Substituting this relationship back into our definition of 𝒞θ​(y∗,y′)\mathcal{C}_{\theta}(y^{*},y^{\prime}) yields:

𝒞θ​(y∗,y′)≈⟨∇θ​log​p,−p1−p​∇θ​log​p⟩=−p1−p​‖∇θ​log​p‖2\mathcal{C}_{\theta}(y^{*},y^{\prime})\approx\left\langle\nabla_{\theta}\log p,-\frac{p}{1-p}\nabla_{\theta}\log p\right\rangle=-\frac{p}{1-p}\|\nabla_{\theta}\log p\|^{2}

This confirms our first structural property: under proportional decay, the inner product of the ground truth and rival log-gradients is strictly negative. The parameter updates inherently oppose each other. We can now substitute this back into the full expansion (Equation 31):

⟨gdiag,ϵvec⟩≈−(w⁡(p,ϕ)p~​p1−p​‖∇θ​log​p‖2)⏟Strictly Non-Negative Constant ​C∑y′∈ℛπθ(y′|x)∂p~∂πθ​(y′|x)\langle g_{\text{diag}},\epsilon_{\text{vec}}\rangle\approx-\underbrace{\left(\frac{w(p,\phi)}{\tilde{p}}\frac{p}{1-p}\|\nabla_{\theta}\log p\|^{2}\right)}_{\text{Strictly Non-Negative Constant }C}\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}}\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}|x)\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}|x)}

This formulation explicitly isolates the effect of the proportional decay assumption. Because the term inside the parentheses, CC, is strictly non-negative, the leading negative sign dictates that the off-diagonal error aligns with our descent direction (⟨gdiag,ϵvec⟩≥0\langle g_{\text{diag}},\epsilon_{\text{vec}}\rangle\geq 0) if and only if the remaining summation is non-positive. In other words, proportional decay structurally guarantees that the error vector points in the correct direction, up to the sign of the strategy’s sensitivity to incorrect answers.

To resolve this final sign and guarantee directional alignment, we must categorize the behavior of the test-time strategy itself.

Definition 1 (Competitive Strategy).

A strategy is Competitive if increasing the probability of any incorrect answer strictly decreases (or leaves unchanged) the probability of success. That is, ∂p~∂πθ​(y′∣x)≤0\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}\leq 0 for all y′∈ℛy^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}.

For any competitive strategy, the partial derivative ∂p~∂πθ​(y′|x)\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}|x)} is non-positive. Because the leading negative sign from our proportional decay derivation cancels this non-positive sum, the entire inner product is strictly non-negative: ⟨gdiag,ϵvec⟩≥0\langle g_{\text{diag}},\epsilon_{\text{vec}}\rangle\geq 0.

This synthesis of proportional decay and competitive strategy dynamics yields two powerful guarantees for our optimization process:

  1. 1.

    Directional Alignment: The ignored off-diagonal error actively points in the same general direction as our approximation (⟨gdiag,ϵvec⟩≥0\langle g_{\text{diag}},\epsilon_{\text{vec}}\rangle\geq 0). We are guaranteed not to step in the wrong direction.

  2. 2.

    Conservative Magnitude: Because the error vector aligns with our approximation, our calculated scalar weight strictly underestimates the true learning signal.

Theorem 3 (Directional Alignment and Conservative Bound).

Assuming proportional decay and a competitive test-time strategy, the off-diagonal error aligns with the diagonal approximation (⟨gdiag,ϵvec⟩≥0\langle g_{\text{diag}},\epsilon_{\text{vec}}\rangle\geq 0). Consequently, the diagonal approximation safely underestimates the exact gradient magnitude: ‖gdiag‖≤‖gexact‖\|g_{\text{diag}}\|\leq\|g_{\text{exact}}\|.

Implications for Optimization: The Conservative Gradient Guarantee.

Together, Theorem 2 and Theorem 3 establish the conditions required for the theoretical safety of the diagonal approximation. Theorem 2 dictates that for the approximation to decrease the true loss, the off-diagonal error must not overpower the diagonal gradient. Theorem 3 satisfies and exceeds this requirement by proving that under standard softmax dynamics (proportional decay), the error vector actually points in the same general direction as our approximation (⟨gdiag,ϵvec⟩≥0\langle g_{\text{diag}},\epsilon_{\text{vec}}\rangle\geq 0).

This yields a powerful conclusion: as long as a Test-Time Strategy is Competitive, meaning rival answers actively hinder the ground truth’s chance of success, ignoring the off-diagonal terms does not send the optimizer in the wrong direction. Instead, it creates a conservative underestimate of the true gradient (‖gdiag‖≤‖gexact‖\|g_{\text{diag}}\|\leq\|g_{\text{exact}}\|). In the context of deep reinforcement learning and fine-tuning, where large variance and overshooting are primary causes of policy collapse, this underestimation acts as a natural stabilizer. It guarantees that our computationally efficient scalar approximation is a safe, valid descent direction.

A.9 Diagonal Approximation Analysis for Specific Strategies

In Section A.8, Theorems 2 and 3 established the geometric safety of the diagonal approximation. Specifically, we proved that for competitive strategies under proportional decay, the approximation actively aligns with the descent direction, guaranteeing that it strictly underestimates the true gradient magnitude (‖gdiag‖≤‖gexact‖\|g_{\text{diag}}\|\leq\|g_{\text{exact}}\|).

However, a conservative underestimate is only practically useful if it captures a meaningful portion of the true learning signal. In this section, we transition from high-dimensional vector geometry to a purely scalar analysis to explicitly quantify the magnitude of this off-diagonal error. By formalizing a taxonomy of inference strategies, we derive exact mathematical bounds on our scalar weights w⁡(p,ϕ)w(p,\phi). This allows us to prove exactly how much of the true gradient’s magnitude is preserved across the specific test-time strategies utilized in our experiments.

A.9.1 The Unified Gradient Equation: From Vectors to Scalars

To quantify the exact magnitude of the bound ‖gdiag‖≤‖gexact‖\|g_{\text{diag}}\|\leq\|g_{\text{exact}}\|, we can project the high-dimensional parameter-space gradients into a scalar dimension.

Recall the full expansion of the exact gradient from Section A.8, partitioned into the ground truth probability p=πθ​(y∗∣x)p=\pi_{\theta}(y^{*}\mid x) and the set of incorrect rivals ℛ\mathcal{R}:

gexact=−1p~​[∂p~∂p​∇θp+∑y′∈ℛ∂p~∂πθ​(y′∣x)​∇θπθ​(y′∣x)]g_{\text{exact}}=-\frac{1}{\tilde{p}}\left[\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p}\nabla_{\theta}p+\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}}\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}\nabla_{\theta}\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}\mid x)\right]

To evaluate the summation, we apply the same Proportional Decay Assumption used to prove Theorem 3, substituting the rival gradient ∇θπθ​(y′∣x)≈−πθ​(y′∣x)1−p​∇θp\nabla_{\theta}\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}\mid x)\approx-\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}{1-p}\nabla_{\theta}p:

gexact≈−1p~​[∂p~∂p​∇θp−∑y′∈ℛ∂p~∂πθ​(y′∣x)​πθ​(y′∣x)1−p​∇θp]g_{\text{exact}}\approx-\frac{1}{\tilde{p}}\left[\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p}\nabla_{\theta}p-\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}}\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}{1-p}\nabla_{\theta}p\right]

By factoring out ∇θp\nabla_{\theta}p, we reveal a crucial structural simplification. Under proportional decay, the exact parameter-space gradient is strictly proportional to a single scalar bracket:

gexact≈−1p~​[∂p~∂p−11−p​∑y′∈ℛπθ​(y′∣x)​∂p~∂πθ​(y′∣x)]⏟Total Scalar Derivative ​d​p~d​p​∇θpg_{\text{exact}}\approx-\frac{1}{\tilde{p}}\underbrace{\left[\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p}-\frac{1}{1-p}\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}}\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}\mid x)\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}\right]}_{\text{Total Scalar Derivative }\frac{d\tilde{p}}{dp}}\nabla_{\theta}p

This bracketed term is the total derivative of the success probability, d​p~d​p\frac{d\tilde{p}}{dp}, accounting for both the direct increase in the ground truth and the proportional decay of the rivals.

Since our diagonal approximation is defined purely by the first term (gdiag=−1p~​∂p~∂p​∇θpg_{\text{diag}}=-\frac{1}{\tilde{p}}\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p}\nabla_{\theta}p), the relationship between the magnitude of our approximation and the exact gradient is entirely captured by this scalar equation. We formalize this as the Unified Gradient Equation:

d​p~d​p=∂p~∂p⏟Direct Sensitivity−11−p​∑y′∈ℛπθ​(y′∣x)​∂p~∂πθ​(y′∣x)⏟Rivalry Correction ​𝒞​rival\frac{d\tilde{p}}{dp}=\underbrace{\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p}}_{\text{Direct Sensitivity}}-\underbrace{\frac{1}{1-p}\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}}\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}\mid x)\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}}_{\text{Rivalry Correction }\mathcal{C}{\text{rival}}} (32)

To see how this connects to the previous section:

ϵvec≈(1p~​𝒞rival)​∇θp\epsilon_{\text{vec}}\approx\left(\frac{1}{\tilde{p}}\mathcal{C}_{\text{rival}}\right)\nabla_{\theta}p

By analytically bounding 𝒞rival\mathcal{C}_{\text{rival}} for specific test-time strategies, we can do more than just measure the gradient magnitude; we can bound the Optimization Efficiency of our training step.

In standard gradient descent with learning rate η\eta, the expected first-order reduction in the true loss when taking a step with our diagonal approximation is Δ​ℒdiag≈−η⁡⟨gexact,gdiag⟩\Delta\mathcal{L}_{\text{diag}}\approx-\eta\langle g_{\text{exact}},g_{\text{diag}}\rangle. If we were to take a step with the exact, computationally intractable gradient, the optimal reduction would be Δ​ℒexact≈−η​‖gexact‖2\Delta\mathcal{L}_{\text{exact}}\approx-\eta\|g_{\text{exact}}\|^{2}.

Because both gdiagg_{\text{diag}} and gexactg_{\text{exact}} are strictly proportional to ∇θp\nabla_{\theta}p under the proportional decay assumption, the high-dimensional dot products cleanly factor out ‖∇θp‖2\|\nabla_{\theta}p\|^{2}. The relative efficiency of our approximation ρ\rho reduces to the simple ratio of the scalar derivatives:

ρ=Δ​ℒdiagΔ​ℒexact≈⟨gexact,gdiag⟩‖gexact‖2=∂p~∂pd​p~d​p=Direct SensitivityDirect Sensitivity−𝒞rival\rho=\frac{\Delta\mathcal{L}_{\text{diag}}}{\Delta\mathcal{L}_{\text{exact}}}\approx\frac{\langle g_{\text{exact}},g_{\text{diag}}\rangle}{\|g_{\text{exact}}\|^{2}}=\frac{\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p}}{\frac{d\tilde{p}}{dp}}=\frac{\text{Direct Sensitivity}}{\text{Direct Sensitivity}-\mathcal{C}_{\text{rival}}} (33)

This efficiency ratio ρ\rho represents the fraction of the optimal loss reduction captured by our computationally cheap proxy. By bounding 𝒞rival\mathcal{C}_{\text{rival}}, we can mathematically guarantee the worst-case optimization efficiency of CAT across different inference strategies.

A.9.2 Strategy Classes

In the previous section, we established that Competitive strategies guarantee a conservative underestimate of the true gradient. To precisely quantify the optimization efficiency ρ\rho and bound the rivalry correction 𝒞rival\mathcal{C}_{\text{rival}}, we introduce two further classifications based on a strategy’s sensitivity to the distribution of incorrect answers 𝝅ℛ\boldsymbol{\pi}_{\mathcal{R}}.

Definition 2 (Orthogonal Strategy).

A strategy is Orthogonal if the success probability is completely invariant to the distribution of incorrect answers. That is, ∇𝝅ℛp~=𝟎\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\pi}_{\mathcal{R}}}\tilde{p}=\mathbf{0}.

Definition 3 (Adversarial Symmetry).

A strategy exhibits Adversarial Symmetry if the sensitivity of the success probability to the strongest possible rival is bounded by its sensitivity to the ground truth. This means that changing the probability of the correct answer has more effect on test-time success than changing any other answer. That is:

maxy′∈ℛ⁡|∂p~∂πθ​(y′∣x)|≤∂p~∂p\max_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}}\left|\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}\right|\leq\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p} (34)

A.9.3 Approximation Theorems

We now apply these classifications to the Unified Gradient Equation to show exactly how much signal is captured, or lost, by the scalar approximation, directly connecting these bounds to the optimization efficiency ρ\rho.

Theorem 4 (Exactness for Orthogonal Strategies).

For any Orthogonal strategy, the total derivative exactly equals the partial derivative (d​p~d​p=∂p~∂p\frac{d\tilde{p}}{dp}=\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p}), resulting in perfect optimization efficiency (ρ=1\rho=1).

Proof.

By Definition 1, the partial derivative with respect to any specific rival y′y^{\prime} is zero. Consequently, the rivalry correction term vanishes (𝒞rival=0\mathcal{C}_{\text{rival}}=0), leaving only the direct sensitivity. Substituting this into our efficiency ratio yields ρ=1\rho=1. Pass@NN is a clear example of an Orthogonal strategy, as success depends exclusively on the presence of the ground truth. ∎

Theorem 5 (The Bounded Gradient Theorem).

For any strategy that is both Competitive and Adversarially Symmetric, the true total derivative of the success probability is strictly bounded by the partial derivative and twice its value:

∂p~∂p≤d​p~d​p≤2​∂p~∂p\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p}\leq\frac{d\tilde{p}}{dp}\leq 2\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p}

Consequently, the optimization efficiency is mathematically guaranteed to remain above 50% (ρ≥0.5\rho\geq 0.5) and safely not overestimate the gradient.

Proof.

From the Unified Gradient Equation (Equation 32), we have d​p~d​p=∂p~∂p+𝒞rival\frac{d\tilde{p}}{dp}=\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p}+\mathcal{C}_{\text{rival}}.

Lower Bound: As established in Theorem 3, the partial derivative for any rival in a Competitive strategy is non-positive (∂p~∂πθ​(y′∣x)≤0\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}\leq 0). Because probabilities are strictly non-negative, the entire rivalry correction term 𝒞rival≥0\mathcal{C}_{\text{rival}}\geq 0. Therefore, d​p~d​p≥∂p~∂p\frac{d\tilde{p}}{dp}\geq\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p}. This is the scalar realization of Theorem 3: the error aligns with our objective, proving the diagonal approximation is a safe, conservative underestimate.

Upper Bound: The correction term 𝒞rival\mathcal{C}_{\text{rival}} reaches its maximum when the entire incorrect probability mass (1−p)(1-p) is concentrated on the single strongest rival ym​a​x′y^{\prime}_{max} (a configuration we term "The Duel"). Substituting this concentration yields 𝒞rival≤|∂p~∂πθ​(ym​a​x′∣x)|\mathcal{C}_{\text{rival}}\leq\left|\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}_{max}\mid x)}\right|. By Adversarial Symmetry, this term is bounded by ∂p~∂p\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p}. Thus, the total derivative cannot exceed ∂p~∂p+∂p~∂p=2​∂p~∂p\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p}+\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p}=2\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p}.

Substituting these derivative bounds back into our efficiency ratio ρ\rho demonstrates that ρ=(∂p~∂p)/(d​p~d​p)≥0.5\rho=(\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p})/(\frac{d\tilde{p}}{dp})\geq 0.5. ∎

Corollary 4 (Majority Vote Approximation Bounds).

Majority Vote is both Competitive and Adversarially Symmetric. Therefore, its scalar approximation safely satisfies Theorem 2 and Theorem 3, guaranteeing a worst-case optimization efficiency of at least 50% (ρ≥0.5\rho\geq 0.5):

∂p~maj∂p≤d​p~majd​p≤2​∂p~maj∂p\frac{\partial\tilde{p}_{\text{maj}}}{\partial p}\leq\frac{d\tilde{p}_{\text{maj}}}{dp}\leq 2\frac{\partial\tilde{p}_{\text{maj}}}{\partial p}
Proof.

Majority Vote is inherently Competitive; increasing the probability of a rival reaching the consensus threshold strictly reduces the win probability of the ground truth.

To prove that Majority Vote satisfies Adversarial Symmetry, let index 00 denote the ground truth y∗y^{*}, and indices j∈{1,…,M}j\in\{1,\dots,M\} denote rival answers. Let WW be the set of vote count configurations 𝐧\mathbf{n} that result in a plurality win for the ground truth. We first derive an exact identity for the partial derivatives of the success probability p~\tilde{p}.

Derivation of the Gradient Identity.

The success probability p~​(𝝅)\tilde{p}(\boldsymbol{\pi}) for an inference budget NN is a polynomial sum over all possible outcome count vectors 𝐧\mathbf{n} such that ∑ni=N\sum n_{i}=N:

p~​(𝝅)=∑𝐧≥0|𝐧|=NN!∏ni!​(∏i=0Mπini)​𝕀​(𝐧∈W)\tilde{p}(\boldsymbol{\pi})=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{n}\geq 0\\ |\mathbf{n}|=N\end{subarray}}\frac{N!}{\prod n_{i}!}\left(\prod_{i=0}^{M}\pi_{i}^{n_{i}}\right)\mathbb{I}(\mathbf{n}\in W) (35)

Differentiating with respect to a specific component πk\pi_{k} yields:

∂p~∂πk=∑𝐧≥0|𝐧|=N,nk≥1N!∏ni!​𝕀​(𝐧∈W)​(nk​πknk−1)​∏i≠kπini\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial\pi_{k}}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{n}\geq 0\\ |\mathbf{n}|=N,n_{k}\geq 1\end{subarray}}\frac{N!}{\prod n_{i}!}\mathbb{I}(\mathbf{n}\in W)(n_{k}\pi_{k}^{n_{k}-1})\prod_{i\neq k}\pi_{i}^{n_{i}} (36)

Using the factorial identity nk​N!nk!=N​(N−1)!(nk−1)!n_{k}\frac{N!}{n_{k}!}=N\frac{(N-1)!}{(n_{k}-1)!}, we can perform a change of variables by shifting the index to 𝐦=𝐧−ek\mathbf{m}=\mathbf{n}-e_{k}, where eke_{k} is the one-hot vector for candidate kk. This transforms the summation into an expectation over an (N−1)(N-1) sample process:

∂p~∂πk\displaystyle\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial\pi_{k}} =N​∑𝐦≥0|𝐦|=N−1(N−1)!∏mi!​∏πimi⏟PMF of Multi​(N−1,𝝅)​𝕀​(𝐦+ek∈W)\displaystyle=N\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{m}\geq 0\\ |\mathbf{m}|=N-1\end{subarray}}\underbrace{\frac{(N-1)!}{\prod m_{i}!}\prod\pi_{i}^{m_{i}}}_{\text{PMF of Multi}(N-1,\boldsymbol{\pi})}\mathbb{I}(\mathbf{m}+e_{k}\in W)
=N⋅Pr⁡(𝐦+ek∈W)\displaystyle=N\cdot\Pr(\mathbf{m}+e_{k}\in W) (37)

This identity is remarkably intuitive: the sensitivity of the success probability to candidate kk is exactly proportional to the probability that the system wins given that we force the NN-th vote to be for candidate kk. This identity holds for any strategy using aggregation by redefining WW.

Establishing Symmetry.

We now apply this identity to compare the sensitivity of the ground truth (k=0k=0) against a rival (k=jk=j).

Let ℰ0={𝐦∣𝐦+e0∈W}\mathcal{E}_{0}=\{\mathbf{m}\mid\mathbf{m}+e_{0}\in W\} be the event that the ground truth wins if it receives the forced NN-th vote. Similarly, let ℰj={𝐦∣𝐦+ej∈W}\mathcal{E}_{j}=\{\mathbf{m}\mid\mathbf{m}+e_{j}\in W\} be the event that the ground truth wins even if the rival jj receives the forced NN-th vote.

Consider any vote configuration 𝐦∈ℰj\mathbf{m}\in\mathcal{E}_{j}. For the ground truth to win despite the rival receiving an extra vote, the ground truth count m0m_{0} must strictly exceed the rival’s augmented count (m0>mj+1m_{0}>m_{j}+1). This is a strictly stronger condition than what is required for ℰ0\mathcal{E}_{0}, which only requires the ground truth’s augmented count to exceed the rival’s count (m0+1>mjm_{0}+1>m_{j}).

Because satisfying the conditions for ℰj\mathcal{E}_{j} inherently satisfies the conditions for ℰ0\mathcal{E}_{0}, we have ℰj⊆ℰ0\mathcal{E}_{j}\subseteq\mathcal{E}_{0}. Since winning under a disadvantage is a subset of winning under an advantage, the probabilities satisfy Pr⁡(ℰj)≤Pr⁡(ℰ0)\Pr(\mathcal{E}_{j})\leq\Pr(\mathcal{E}_{0}).

Multiplying by NN recovers the gradient inequality, proving that Majority Vote satisfies Adversarial Symmetry:

|∂p~∂πj|≤∂p~∂π0\left|\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial\pi_{j}}\right|\leq\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial\pi_{0}} (38)

∎

A.10 Relaxing the Competitive Assumption: Guarantees under Adversarial Symmetry

In Theorem 3, we established that for Competitive strategies, the off-diagonal error vector strictly aligns with our diagonal approximation (⟨gdiag,ϵvec⟩≥0\langle g_{\text{diag}},\epsilon_{\text{vec}}\rangle\geq 0), guaranteeing a safe underestimate of the true gradient. However, certain complex test-time strategies may not be strictly Competitive. If increasing the probability of a rival answer y′y^{\prime} might increase the overall success probability (∂p~∂πθ​(y′∣x)>0\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}>0), the error vector may actively oppose the diagonal update.

We must therefore ensure that this opposing force does not overpower the intended descent direction. We demonstrate that non competitive strategies with Adversarial Symmetry satisfy the descent conditions of Theorem 2.

Theorem 6 (Fail-Safe Descent under Adversarial Symmetry).

Assume the generation process follows Proportional Decay. For any test-time strategy satisfying Adversarial Symmetry, the magnitude of the off-diagonal error vector is bounded by the magnitude of the diagonal gradient approximation:

‖ϵvec‖≤‖gdiag‖\|\epsilon_{\text{vec}}\|\leq\|g_{\text{diag}}\| (39)

Consequently, optimizing via the diagonal approximation is guaranteed never to ascend the exact objective landscape, regardless of whether the strategy is Competitive.

Proof.

Recall the full expansion of the exact gradient under the Proportional Decay assumption:

gexact=gdiag+ϵvecg_{\text{exact}}=g_{\text{diag}}+\epsilon_{\text{vec}} (40)

where the diagonal gradient is defined as gdiag=−1p~​∂p~∂p​∇θpg_{\text{diag}}=-\frac{1}{\tilde{p}}\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p}\nabla_{\theta}p, and the off-diagonal error vector is:

ϵvec=1p~​[11−p​∑y′∈ℛπθ​(y′∣x)​∂p~∂πθ​(y′∣x)]​∇θp\epsilon_{\text{vec}}=\frac{1}{\tilde{p}}\left[\frac{1}{1-p}\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}}\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}\mid x)\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}\right]\nabla_{\theta}p (41)

To determine if the error vector can overpower our approximation, we analyze its maximum magnitude using the triangle inequality:

‖ϵvec‖≤1p~​11−p​∑y′∈ℛπθ​(y′∣x)​|∂p~∂πθ​(y′∣x)|​‖∇θp‖\|\epsilon_{\text{vec}}\|\leq\frac{1}{\tilde{p}}\frac{1}{1-p}\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}}\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}\mid x)\left|\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}\right|\|\nabla_{\theta}p\| (42)

By adversarial symmetry, the absolute sensitivity of the success probability to any rival is strictly bounded by its sensitivity to the ground truth: |∂p~∂πθ​(y′∣x)|≤∂p~∂p\left|\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}\right|\leq\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p}. Substituting this upper bound into the summation yields:

‖ϵvec‖≤1p~​11−p​(∂p~∂p)​‖∇θp‖​∑y′∈ℛπθ​(y′∣x)\|\epsilon_{\text{vec}}\|\leq\frac{1}{\tilde{p}}\frac{1}{1-p}\left(\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p}\right)\|\nabla_{\theta}p\|\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}}\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}\mid x) (43)

The sum of the probabilities of all rival answers is exactly the remaining probability mass: ∑y′∈ℛπθ​(y′∣x)=1−p\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}}\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}\mid x)=1-p. Substituting this into the inequality perfectly cancels the denominator:

‖ϵvec‖≤1p~​∂p~∂p​‖∇θp‖=‖gdiag‖\|\epsilon_{\text{vec}}\|\leq\frac{1}{\tilde{p}}\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p}\|\nabla_{\theta}p\|=\|g_{\text{diag}}\| (44)

This completes the proof. ∎

Implications for Optimization.

Theorem 2 established that a strict bound (‖ϵvec‖<‖gdiag‖\|\epsilon_{\text{vec}}\|<\|g_{\text{diag}}\|) guarantees a strict decrease in the true loss. Under Theorem 6, this strict bound holds in all typical cases. The equality ‖ϵvec‖=‖gdiag‖\|\epsilon_{\text{vec}}\|=\|g_{\text{diag}}\| is only achieved in the worst-case scenario where the entirety of the incorrect probability mass (1−p)(1-p) is concentrated on a single, maximally adversarial rival, and the strategy is entirely non-competitive. In that extreme edge case, the opposing error exactly cancels the diagonal update (gexact=𝟎g_{\text{exact}}=\mathbf{0}). Thus, the diagonal approximation provides a robust guarantee: it strictly minimizes the loss in typical scenarios and safely stalls in worst-case scenarios, preventing the optimizer from stepping in the wrong direction.

A.11 Empirical Validation of the Diagonal Approximation for Majority Vote

To understand beyond the theory how good the diagonal approximation is on average, we empirically measure the optimization efficiency (ρ\rho) of our diagonal approximation during training. While guarantees that ignoring the off-diagonal rivalry terms 𝒞r​i​v​a​l\mathcal{C}_{rival} preserves the correct directional gradient and bounds the magnitude loss (ρ≥0.5\rho\geq 0.5 for Majority Vote), we want to empirically understand how good our approximation is.

Methodology.

We evaluate a Mistral-7B-Instruct model fine tuned on 2000 problems on a validation subset of the MATH benchmark. For each problem, we generate M=32M=32 candidate solutions to establish an empirical distribution over the sequence-level probabilities of both the ground truth (πθ​(y∗|x)\pi_{\theta}(y^{*}|x)) and the set of incorrect rival answers (ℛ\mathcal{R}). To compute the intractable off-diagonal sensitivities ∂p~∂πθ​(y′|x)\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}|x)}, we utilize the combinatorial identity ∂p~∂πθ​(y′|x)=N⋅P​r​(y∗​ wins∣y′​ receives 1 free vote)\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}|x)}=N\cdot Pr(y^{*}\text{ wins}\mid y^{\prime}\text{ receives 1 free vote}) and estimate it via the Monte Carlo simulation for a test-time budget of N=8N=8. The empirical optimization efficiency is then calculated as the ratio of the diagonal term to the full exact derivative:

ρ=∂p~∂p∂p~∂p+𝒞r​i​v​a​l\rho=\frac{\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p}}{\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p}+\mathcal{C}_{rival}}
Results & Analysis.

As shown in Figure 9, the empirical measurements follow our theoretical bounds. Across the evaluated distribution, the optimization efficiency never violates the theoretical lower bound of ρ≥0.50\rho\geq 0.50. Furthermore, the empirical average efficiency is ρ=0.8633\rho=0.8633. This indicates that, in practice, the diagonal approximation captures over 86%86\% of the true gradient signal magnitude.
