This high empirical ρ\rho value is highly consequential for test-time alignment. It demonstrates that the computationally prohibitive task of evaluating the full parameter-space Jacobian across all rival sequences is unnecessary. By employing the diagonal approximation, we achieve a highly efficient surrogate objective for SFT and RL that faithfully represents the true test-time Majority Vote objective, simultaneously reducing variance and eliminating the need for exhaustive rival sampling during training.

Appendix B Derivations and Explanations for RL

B.1 RL Gradient Estimation

For RL, we do not assume access to labeled data but instead learn from a general reward function R⁡(y|x)R(y|x). Our derivation is very similar to [24].

The classic RL REINFORCE objective [25] maximizes the expected reward of a single generation under the base policy:

J(θ)=𝔼y∼πθ(⋅∣x)[R(y|x)]=∑y∈𝒴πθ(y∣x)R(y|x)J(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)}[R(y|x)]=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)R(y|x) (45)

To align this objective with a Test-Time Strategy (TTS), we elevate the expectation to operate over the effective system-level policy. Let π~θ​(y∣x)=𝒯⁡(πθ,ϕ)​(y∣x)\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(y\mid x)=\mathcal{T}(\pi_{\theta},\phi)(y\mid x) denote the probability that the overall system selects yy as its final output.

The CAT objective for RL is the expected reward under the test-time strategy:

JCAT(θ)=𝔼y∼π~θ(⋅∣x)[R(y|x)]=∑y∈𝒴π~θ(y∣x)R(y|x)J_{\text{CAT}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)}[R(y|x)]=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(y\mid x)R(y|x) (46)

We compute the gradient with respect to θ\theta.

Let 𝝅θ\boldsymbol{\pi}_{\theta} denote the vector of base probabilities over the output space 𝒴\mathcal{Y}. The gradient of the objective is:

∇θJCAT=∑y∈𝒴R⁡(y|x)​∇θπ~θ​(y|x)\nabla_{\theta}J_{\text{CAT}}=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}R(y|x)\nabla_{\theta}\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(y|x) (47)

Expanding ∇θπ~θ​(y|x)\nabla_{\theta}\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(y|x) :

∇θπ~​(y|x)=∑y′∈𝒴∂π~θ​(y|x)∂πθ​(y′|x)​∇θπθ​(y′|x)\nabla_{\theta}\tilde{\pi}(y|x)=\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}}\frac{\partial\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(y|x)}{\partial\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}|x)}\nabla_{\theta}\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}|x) (48)

Substituting this back into the objective and swapping the order of summation:

∇θJCAT\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}J_{\text{CAT}} =∑y∈𝒴R⁡(y|x)​(∑y′∈𝒴∂π~θ​(y|x)∂πθ​(y′|x)​∇θπθ​(y′|x))\displaystyle=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}R(y|x)\left(\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}}\frac{\partial\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(y|x)}{\partial\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}|x)}\nabla_{\theta}\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}|x)\right)
=∑y′∈𝒴(∑y∈𝒴R⁡(y|x)​∂π~θ​(y|x)∂πθ​(y′|x))​∇θπθ​(y′|x)\displaystyle=\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}}\left(\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}R(y|x)\frac{\partial\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(y|x)}{\partial\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}|x)}\right)\nabla_{\theta}\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}|x) (49)

Using the log-derivative trick ∇θπθ​(y′)=πθ​(y′)​∇θ​log⁡πθ​(y′)\nabla_{\theta}\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime})=\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime})\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}), we can express this as an expectation over the base policy:

∇θJCAT=𝔼y′∼πθ​[(∑y∈𝒴R⁡(y|x)​∂π~θ​(y|x)∂πθ​(y′|x))⏟Marginal Test-Time Reward​∇θ​log⁡πθ​(y′|x)]\nabla_{\theta}J_{\text{CAT}}=\mathbb{E}_{y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\theta}}\left[\underbrace{\left(\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}R(y|x)\frac{\partial\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(y|x)}{\partial\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}|x)}\right)}_{\text{Marginal Test-Time Reward}}\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}|x)\right] (50)

Equation 50 is the exact gradient. We will make the same assumption as the SFT case, that π~θ​(y|x)\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(y|x) is a function of πθ​(y|x)\pi_{\theta}(y|x):

∂π~θ​(y|x)∂πθ​(y′|x)≈{∂π~θ​(y|x)∂πθ​(y|x)if ​y=y′0if ​y≠y′\frac{\partial\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(y|x)}{\partial\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}|x)}\approx\begin{cases}\frac{\partial\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(y|x)}{\partial\pi_{\theta}(y|x)}&\text{if }y=y^{\prime}\\ 0&\text{if }y\neq y^{\prime}\end{cases} (51)

Letting p=πθ​(y|x)p=\pi_{\theta}(y|x) and p~=π~θ​(y|x)\tilde{p}=\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(y|x), the gradient simplifies to:

∇θJCAT≈𝔼y∼πθ​[(R⁡(y|x)​∂p~∂p)​∇θ​log⁡πθ​(y|x)]\nabla_{\theta}J_{\text{CAT}}\approx\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta}}\left[\left(R(y|x)\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p}\right)\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y|x)\right] (52)

The standard reward R⁡(y|x)R(y|x) is effectively multiplied by the marginal increase in test-time probability ∂p~∂p\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p}. We define R~\tilde{R} such that R​(y|x)​∂p~∂p=R~​(y|x)R(y|x)\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p}=\tilde{R}(y|x).

B.2 RL Strategy Instantiations

We derive the specific gradient estimators for the three primary test-time strategies with MM rollouts. The update takes the form of a weighted policy gradient:

∇θJ≈1M​∑i=1MR~​(yi|x)⋅∇θ​log​πθ​(yi∣x)\nabla_{\theta}J\approx\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}\tilde{R}(y_{i}|x)\cdot\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{i}\mid x) (53)

B.2.1 Pass@NN

Recall that p~\tilde{p} for Pass@NN is 1−(1−p)N1-(1-p)^{N} but this is only if the answer we chose is a correct one which was implicitly always true for SFT, otherwise the probability of the answer getting chosen is 00. Luckily, if the answer is incorrect, R⁡(yi|x)R(y_{i}|x) is 00 anyways.

Thus the RL update weight for a sample yiy_{i} is:

R~pass​(yi|x)=R⁡(yi|x)⋅N​(1−p)N−1\tilde{R}_{\text{pass}}(y_{i}|x)=R(y_{i}|x)\cdot N(1-p)^{N-1} (54)

B.2.2 Majority Vote (Dynamic Threshold)

Previously, we computed p~=∑i=kN(Ni)​pi​(1−p)N−i\tilde{p}=\sum_{i=k}^{N}\binom{N}{i}p^{i}(1-p)^{N-i} and ∂p~∂p=N​(N−1k−1)​pk−1​(1−p)N−k\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{{\partial p}}=N\binom{N-1}{k-1}p^{k-1}(1-p)^{N-k} with kk being the threshold required for the answer to be chosen. Previously, we had chosen kk as a hyperparameter. We could still do that. However, here, since we are sampling alternative answers, we can estimate kk using the batch.

Let qi^\hat{q_{i}} be the empirical probability of the most common alternate answer to yiy_{i} in our MM rollouts. For the correct answer to win in an inference budget of NN, it must appear at least kk times, where:

k^i≈⌊N⋅q^⌋+1\hat{k}_{i}\approx\lfloor N\cdot\hat{q}\rfloor+1

This establishes a dynamic threshold kk based on the "strength of the opposition."

B.2.3 Best-of-NN (Empirical Max Reward)

In this setting, the strategy samples NN candidates {y1,…,yN}\{y_{1},\dots,y_{N}\} and selects the candidate with the maximum reward y~=arg​maxyi⁡R​(yi|x)\tilde{y}=\argmax_{y_{i}}R(y_{i}|x).

To compute p~\tilde{p} as a function of pp. Let the rollout batch of MM candidates be sorted by reward. For a specific output yy, let P<yP_{<y} denote the probability of generating an answer with a reward strictly lower than R⁡(y|x)R(y|x). The probability that a specific candidate yy is the selected maximum corresponds to the likelihood that all NN sampled candidates have rewards less than or equal to R⁡(y|x)R(y|x), excluding the scenario where all candidates have rewards strictly less than R⁡(y|x)R(y|x). The probability that yy wins is given by:

p~​(y)=(P<y+p⁡(y))N−(P<y)N\tilde{p}(y)=(P_{<y}+p(y))^{N}-(P_{<y})^{N} (55)

To derive the gradient with respect to p⁡(y)p(y), we must enforce the constraint that probability distributions sum to 1. We assume that an increase in p⁡(y)p(y) is achieved by transferring probability mass from worse answers (P<yP_{<y}), while the probability of strictly better answers (P>yP_{>y}) remains constant.

Under this assumption, the cumulative probability of answers ≤y\leq y is constant relative to local changes in p⁡(y)p(y):

P≤y=P<y+p⁡(y)=constP_{\leq y}=P_{<y}+p(y)=\text{const}

Rearranging for P<yP_{<y}, we have P<y=P≤y−p⁡(y)P_{<y}=P_{\leq y}-p(y). Substituting this into the objective function:

p~​(y)=(P≤y)N−(P≤y−p⁡(y))N\tilde{p}(y)=(P_{\leq y})^{N}-(P_{\leq y}-p(y))^{N} (56)

Differentiating with respect to p⁡(y)p(y):

∂p~​(y)∂p⁡(y)\displaystyle\frac{\partial\tilde{p}(y)}{\partial p(y)} =0−N​(P≤y−p⁡(y))N−1⋅(−1)\displaystyle=0-N(P_{\leq y}-p(y))^{N-1}\cdot(-1)
=N​(P<y)N−1\displaystyle=N(P_{<y})^{N-1} (57)

This result implies that the gradient signal is proportional to the probability that all competing samples are strictly worse than the current candidate yy.

We estimate P<yP_{<y} empirically using the rollout batch. Let c>yc_{>y} be the count of samples with reward greater than yy, and c=yc_{=y} be the count equal to yy. Then P<y≈1−c>y+c=yMP_{<y}\approx 1-\frac{c_{>y}+c_{=y}}{M}.

The advantage weighting for the policy gradient update becomes:

R~BoN​(yi|x)=R⁡(yi|x)⋅N​(1−c>yi+c=yiM)N−1\tilde{R}_{\text{BoN}}(y_{i}|x)=R(y_{i}|x)\cdot N\left(1-\frac{c_{>y_{i}}+c_{=y_{i}}}{M}\right)^{N-1} (58)
Reduction to Pass@NN:

Consider the binary case where R⁡(y)∈{0,1}R(y)\in\{0,1\}.

  • •

    Correct Answer (R=1R=1): Here, c>y=0c_{>y}=0 and c=y=ccorrectc_{=y}=c_{\text{correct}}. The estimated lower-tail mass is 1−p^1-\hat{p}. The weight becomes:

    A=1⋅N​(1−p^)N−1A=1\cdot N(1-\hat{p})^{N-1}

    This matches Pass@NN but with pp computed using the empirical probabilities of the batch.

  • •

    Incorrect Answer (R=0R=0): Here, all samples are either equal (0) or better (1), so c>y+c=y=Mc_{>y}+c_{=y}=M. The term becomes (1−1)N−1=0(1-1)^{N-1}=0, correctly resulting in zero reward for incorrect answers.

B.3 Best-of-N: Diagonal Approximation Guarantees

Under the assumptions we have made, BoN demonstrates Adversarial Symmetry, allowing us to claim that the diagonal approximation is a safe underestimate. To see this, we must analyze the sensitivity of its test-time success probability to both the ground truth sequence yy and any rival sequence y′y^{\prime}.

Recall the effective probability of selecting sequence yy under Best-of-N:

p~​(y)=(P≤y)N−(P<y)N\tilde{p}(y)=(P_{\leq y})^{N}-(P_{<y})^{N} (59)

The direct sensitivity with respect to the ground truth probability p⁡(y)p(y) is:

∂p~​(y)∂p⁡(y)=N​(P≤y)N−1\frac{\partial\tilde{p}(y)}{\partial p(y)}=N(P_{\leq y})^{N-1} (60)

Next, we evaluate the partial derivative with respect to a rival sequence y′y^{\prime}. We consider two cases based on the reward R⁡(y′)R(y^{\prime}):

  • •

    Stronger Rival (R⁡(y′)>R⁡(y)R(y^{\prime})>R(y)): The probability p⁡(y′)p(y^{\prime}) does not contribute to P≤yP_{\leq y} or P<yP_{<y}. Therefore, the derivative is 00.

  • •

    Weaker Rival (R⁡(y′)<R⁡(y)R(y^{\prime})<R(y)): The probability p⁡(y′)p(y^{\prime}) is included in both P≤yP_{\leq y} and P<yP_{<y}. Taking the derivative yields:

    ∂p~​(y)∂p⁡(y′)=N​(P≤y)N−1−N​(P<y)N−1\frac{\partial\tilde{p}(y)}{\partial p(y^{\prime})}=N(P_{\leq y})^{N-1}-N(P_{<y})^{N-1} (61)

A strategy exhibits Adversarial Symmetry if the absolute sensitivity to any rival is strictly bounded by the sensitivity to the ground truth:

maxy′∈ℛ⁡|∂p~∂p⁡(y′)|≤∂p~∂p⁡(y)\max_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}}\left|\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p(y^{\prime})}\right|\leq\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p(y)} (62)

Comparing the maximum rival sensitivity to the direct sensitivity, we have:

N​(P≤y)N−1−N​(P<y)N−1≤N​(P≤y)N−1N(P_{\leq y})^{N-1}-N(P_{<y})^{N-1}\leq N(P_{\leq y})^{N-1} (63)

Because probability distributions are strictly non-negative (P<y≥0P_{<y}\geq 0), this inequality strictly holds.

Therefore, Best-of-N inherently satisfies Adversarial Symmetry. Consequently, the diagonal approximation for Best-of-N mathematically guarantees fail-safe descent (‖ϵv​e​c‖≤‖gd​i​a​g‖||\epsilon_{vec}||\leq||g_{diag}||). This ensures that the scalar approximation acts in the same direction of the true gradient, preventing the optimizer from stepping in the wrong direction.

Uncompetitiveness.

We can make further guarantees about the approximation. Because probability distributions are strictly non-negative, P≤y>P<yP_{\leq y}>P_{<y}. Consequently, the sensitivity to any weaker rival is strictly positive (∂p~∂p⁡(y′)>0\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p(y^{\prime})}>0). Intuitively, increasing the likelihood of generating a weaker answer effectively "pads" the batch with easy opponents, increasing the ground truth’s chance of surviving the tournament. Because rival sensitivities are strictly nonnegative, Best-of-NN is formally classified as an Uncompetitive Strategy.

Because the strategy is uncompetitive, the rivalry correction term 𝒞r​i​v​a​l\mathcal{C}_{rival} from the Unified Gradient Equation (Equation 32) evaluates to a strictly positive value. Since the exact total derivative is d​p~d​p=∂p~∂p−𝒞r​i​v​a​l\frac{d\tilde{p}}{dp}=\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p}-\mathcal{C}_{rival}, the exact gradient magnitude is smaller than our diagonal term. Thus, the diagonal approximation strictly overestimates the true gradient (ρ≥1.0\rho\geq 1.0). This is a worse situation than a conservative underestimate. Thus, it is advised to decrease learning rate with BoN CAT training.

B.4 Empirical Accuracy of BoN Diagonal Approximation

We may have a theoretical guarantee that the diagonal approximation points in the right direction; however, we have no such guarantee of efficiency. We empirically demonstrate the efficacy of this approximation. To do this experiment, we must quantify the magnitude of the discarded rivalry correction 𝒞r​i​v​a​l\mathcal{C}_{rival}.

B.5 Derivation of Rival Sensitivity

To circumvent the intractable Jacobian evaluation, we exploit the mathematical structure of independent test-time sampling. Because BoN draws NN independent samples from the categorical distribution defined by πθ(⋅|x)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x), the resulting counts of each generated sequence follow a multinomial distribution. This derivation is virtually identitcal to the one done for Section A.9.3.

Let C=(c1,c2,…,cK)C=(c_{1},c_{2},\dots,c_{K}) be the counts of all possible sequences, such that ∑ci=N\sum c_{i}=N. The probability of any specific batch configuration is:

ℙ⁡(C)=N!∏ici!​∏iπθ​(yi|x)ci\mathbb{P}(C)=\frac{N!}{\prod_{i}c_{i}!}\prod_{i}\pi_{\theta}(y_{i}|x)^{c_{i}} (64)

Let WW be the set of all batch configurations where y∗y^{*} wins the BoN tournament (i.e., cy∗≥1c_{y^{*}}\geq 1 and R⁡(y∗|x)≥R⁡(yi|x)R(y^{*}|x)\geq R(y_{i}|x) for all drawn yiy_{i}). The total success probability is p~=∑C∈Wℙ⁡(C)\tilde{p}=\sum_{C\in W}\mathbb{P}(C).

When we take the partial derivative of p~\tilde{p} with respect to a specific rival sequence’s probability πθ​(y′|x)\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}|x), the exponent cy′c_{y^{\prime}} is brought down as a multiplier. Through factorial cancellation, the NN terms rearrange perfectly to describe an (N−1)(N-1) multinomial distribution, mapping the derivative exactly to a conditional expectation:

∂p~∂πθ​(y′|x)\displaystyle\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}|x)} =∑C∈Wcy′​(N!c1!​…​cy′!​…​cK!)​πθ​(y1|x)c1​…​πθ​(y′|x)cy′−1​…\displaystyle=\sum_{C\in W}c_{y^{\prime}}\left(\frac{N!}{c_{1}!\dots c_{y^{\prime}}!\dots c_{K}!}\right)\pi_{\theta}(y_{1}|x)^{c_{1}}\dots\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}|x)^{c_{y^{\prime}}-1}\dots (65)
=N​∑C∈W((N−1)!c1!​…​(cy′−1)!​…​cK!)​∏iπθ​(yi|x)c~i\displaystyle=N\sum_{C\in W}\left(\frac{(N-1)!}{c_{1}!\dots(c_{y^{\prime}}-1)!\dots c_{K}!}\right)\prod_{i}\pi_{\theta}(y_{i}|x)^{\tilde{c}_{i}}
=N⋅ℙ⁡(y∗​ wins BoN∣y′​ receives 1 guaranteed draw)\displaystyle=N\cdot\mathbb{P}\big(y^{*}\text{ wins BoN}\mid y^{\prime}\text{ receives 1 guaranteed draw}\big)

Note again the similarity to the derivation in Section A.9.3.

B.5.1 Empirical Approximation of Optimization Efficiency

Using Equation 65, we can precisely measure the magnitude of the rivalry correction without computing the true Jacobian. By normalizing the probabilities across the empirical candidate space, the rivalry correction becomes the expected conditional sensitivity:

𝒞r​i​v​a​l=11−πθ​(y∗|x)​∑y′≠y∗πθ​(y′|x)​[N⋅ℙ⁡(y∗​ wins∣y′​ guaranteed)]\mathcal{C}_{rival}=\frac{1}{1-\pi_{\theta}(y^{*}|x)}\sum_{y^{\prime}\neq y^{*}}\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}|x)\left[N\cdot\mathbb{P}\big(y^{*}\text{ wins}\mid y^{\prime}\text{ guaranteed}\big)\right] (66)
Results

To empirically validate that our diagonal approximation is not too far off, we approximated ρ\rho across empirical protein sequences using N=8N=8 for our NN in BoN and batch size M=64M=64 using 400 random inputs with the conditional reward experimental setup from Appendix M on the warmed-up SFT model. As shown in Figure 10, our empirical measurements strictly do not stray too far from 11. The empirical average optimization efficiency is ρ≈1.26\rho\approx 1.26. This means that on average our gradient overestimates the true gradient by 1.261.26.

B.6 Variance of the Gradient Estimator

In the Reinforcement Learning setting, the strategy-aware gradient can be viewed as an importance-weighted estimator. Let the standard RL gradient for a single sample be denoted as ∇θJbase≈R⁡(y|x)​∇θ​log⁡πθ​(y|x)\nabla_{\theta}J_{\text{base}}\approx R(y|x)\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y|x). The CAT gradient modifies this with a strategy-specific weight ww:

∇θJCAT≈w⋅∇θJbase\nabla_{\theta}J_{\text{CAT}}\approx w\cdot\nabla_{\theta}J_{\text{base}} (67)

where w=∂p~∂pw=\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p} is the scalar scaling factor derived in previous sections.

To quantify the stability of this estimator, we use the Variance Inflation (VI) factor. Assuming the variance of the gradient is dominated by the magnitude of the scaling coefficients, the inflation relative to standard RL is proportional to the second moment of the weights:

VI≈𝔼⁡[w2]=𝔼⁡[|∂p~∂p|2]\text{VI}\approx\mathbb{E}[w^{2}]=\mathbb{E}\left[\left|\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p}\right|^{2}\right] (68)

We analyze how this variance scales with the inference budget NN across the three primary strategies.

B.6.1 Best-of-NN: Linear Scaling (O⁡(N)O(N))

For Best-of-NN, the weight ww depends on the relative rank (quantile) u∈[0,1]u\in[0,1] of the generated sample’s reward. The weight function is w⁡(u)=N​uN−1w(u)=Nu^{N-1}. Assuming a uniform distribution of quantiles in the rollout batch, the expected squared weight is:

𝔼⁡[w2]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[w^{2}] =∫01(N​uN−1)2​𝑑u=N2​∫01u2​N−2​𝑑u\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{1}\left(Nu^{N-1}\right)^{2}du=N^{2}\int_{0}^{1}u^{2N-2}du
=N2​[u2​N−12​N−1]01=N22​N−1≈N2\displaystyle=N^{2}\left[\frac{u^{2N-1}}{2N-1}\right]_{0}^{1}=\frac{N^{2}}{2N-1}\approx\frac{N}{2} (69)

Result: The variance for Best-of-NN scales linearly with NN. This confirms the "winner-take-all" instability: as NN increases, the effective sample size decreases, concentrating the signal on the top 1/N1/N fraction of samples.

B.6.2 Pass@NN: Quadratic Scaling (O⁡(N2)O(N^{2}))

For Pass@NN, the weight is determined by the prompt difficulty pp. The weight is given by w=N​(1−p)N−1w=N(1-p)^{N-1}.

  • •

    Hard Regime (p≪1/Np\ll 1/N): In this regime, (1−p)N−1≈1(1-p)^{N-1}\approx 1. Consequently, the weight approaches w≈Nw\approx N.

  • •

    Variance: The second moment scales as 𝔼⁡[w2]≈N2\mathbb{E}[w^{2}]\approx N^{2}.

Result: Pass@NN exhibits quadratic variance scaling for hard problems. This makes it the most unstable objective for RL. If the model encounters a batch of hard problems, the gradients scale by N2N^{2}, likely necessitating aggressive gradient clipping to prevent policy collapse.

B.6.3 Majority Vote: Linear Scaling (O⁡(N)O(N))

For Majority Vote, we recall that the derivative of the effective probability corresponds to the probability mass of the Binomial distribution at the decision threshold. Specifically, for a consensus threshold kk, the weight is:

w=∂p~∂p=N​(N−1k−1)​pk−1​(1−p)N−kw=\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p}=N\binom{N-1}{k-1}p^{k-1}(1-p)^{N-k} (70)

The gradient is most active at the decision boundary where the model’s base probability aligns with the requirement, i.e., p≈k/Np\approx k/N.

Let us assume the threshold scales linearly with the budget, such that k≈N/ck\approx N/c for some constant c>1c>1 (e.g., c=2c=2 for simple majority). At the decision boundary, the base probability is p≈1/cp\approx 1/c. We approximate the Binomial term using a Gaussian distribution 𝒩⁡(μ,σ2)\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2}) where the variance is:

σ2=N​p​(1−p)≈N⁡(1c)​(1−1c)\sigma^{2}=Np(1-p)\approx N\left(\frac{1}{c}\right)\left(1-\frac{1}{c}\right) (71)

Crucially, despite the constant cc, the variance scales linearly with the budget: σ2∝N\sigma^{2}\propto N.

At the peak of this distribution (the decision boundary), the probability mass scales inversely with the standard deviation:

(N−1k−1)​pk−1​(1−p)N−k≈12​π​σ2∝1N\binom{N-1}{k-1}p^{k-1}(1-p)^{N-k}\approx\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^{2}}}\propto\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}} (72)

Substituting this back into the expression for the weight ww:

wpeak≈N⋅CN∝Nw_{\text{peak}}\approx N\cdot\frac{C}{\sqrt{N}}\propto\sqrt{N} (73)

The Variance Inflation is determined by the square of this weight:

VI≈𝔼⁡[w2]∝(N)2=N\text{VI}\approx\mathbb{E}[w^{2}]\propto(\sqrt{N})^{2}=N (74)

B.7 Variance Reduction in Gradient Estimation

As derived in the previous subsection, the variance of standard estimators for strategies like Pass@NN can scale quadratically with the inference budget (O⁡(N2)O(N^{2})) in low-probability regimes. To make training stable and efficient, we will describe some tricks we used to reduce variance.

B.7.1 Pass@NN Normalized Weight

The raw RL gradient weight for Pass@NN is given by wRL=N​(1−p)N−1w_{\text{RL}}=N(1-p)^{N-1}. For "hard" samples where p→0p\to 0, this weight causes the variance of the gradient to explode as NN increases.

To remedy this, we adopt the normalized scaling factor derived from our SFT formulation (Section A.2). We replace the raw RL weight with the normalized weight wNormw_{\text{Norm}}:

wNorm=pp~⋅wRL=p1−(1−p)N⋅N​(1−p)N−1w_{\text{Norm}}=\frac{p}{\tilde{p}}\cdot w_{\text{RL}}=\frac{p}{1-(1-p)^{N}}\cdot N(1-p)^{N-1} (75)

From our previous analyses in Section A.6, we know that this weight doesn’t experience a variance explosion.

But, the question remains, how much bias does this weight introduce. To quantify the bias introduced by substituting the normalized weight wNormw_{\text{Norm}} for the true reinforcement learning weight wRLw_{\text{RL}}, we can examine the ratio between the two estimators. This ratio is exactly the scaling factor from our SFT derivation:

wNormwRL=p1−(1−p)N\frac{w_{\text{Norm}}}{w_{\text{RL}}}=\frac{p}{1-(1-p)^{N}} (76)

Because this is a multiplicative factor, the normalized estimator introduces an attenuation bias relative to the exact gradient. The severity of this bias depends directly on the difficulty of the sample:

The Hard Regime (p→0p\to 0):

For highly uncertain generations, we can analyze the asymptotic bias using a first-order Taylor expansion where (1−p)N≈1−N​p(1-p)^{N}\approx 1-Np:

limp→0wNormwRL≈p1−(1−N​p)=1N\lim_{p\to 0}\frac{w_{\text{Norm}}}{w_{\text{RL}}}\approx\frac{p}{1-(1-Np)}=\frac{1}{N} (77)

In the low-probability regime, the normalized estimator systematically underestimates the true gradient magnitude by a factor of NN.

The Easy Regime (p→1p\to 1):

As the model masters a prompt and the base probability approaches certainty, (1−p)N→0(1-p)^{N}\to 0, and the scaling ratio approaches 11:

limp→1wNormwRL=1\lim_{p\to 1}\frac{w_{\text{Norm}}}{w_{\text{RL}}}=1 (78)

Here, the estimator is asymptotically unbiased.

Conclusion: The normalized weight removes the variance explosion but adds bias as p→0p\to 0. However, this bias decreases the magnitude of the gradient, which is preferable to overestimating it to avoid overtraining. We show this emprically in Appendix N.

B.7.2 Parameter Estimation with Small Batches (M≪NM\ll N)

A significant practical challenge in CAT RL is the discrepancy between the training rollout size (MM) and the intended test-time budget (NN). Due to memory constraints, we often set M≪NM\ll N (e.g., M=4M=4 rollouts while optimizing for Pass@6464).

This leads to high variance in the estimation of the strategy parameters, such as the thresholds (for Best-of-NN or Maj Vote). To mitigate this, we sometimes used the following techniques.

Smoothing Empirical Counts.

To prevent the estimates of thresholds from swinging wildly (e.g., between 0 and 1) due to small batch sizes MM, we apply Laplace smoothing:

k^smooth=n+1M+2\hat{k}_{\text{smooth}}=\frac{n+1}{M+2} (79)

where nn is the number of successful outcomes in the batch. This simple adjustment prevents numerical instability and dampens extreme gradient spikes derived from statistically anomalous batches.

Distribution Tracking.

While smoothing addresses numerical stability, it does not solve the issue of coarse granularity. For strategies like Best-of-NN, relying on a small batch size (MM) forces the estimated quantiles P<yP_{<y} to take on discrete, coarse values (e.g., 0,0.25,0.5,…0,0.25,0.5,\dots for M=4M=4). This quantization introduces significant noise into the gradient.

To remedy this, we decouple the estimation of distributional statistics from the immediate mini-batch by maintaining a history buffer or moving average of recent trajectories.

  • •

    For Best-of-NN (Time-Weighted Estimate): To account for non-stationarity (the fact that the model’s reward distribution shifts as it learns), we cannot treat all samples in the history buffer equally. Instead of a uniform average, we employ a time-weighted estimation strategy.

    We maintain a FIFO buffer ℬ\mathcal{B} of pairs (rj,tj)(r_{j},t_{j}), representing the reward and the training step of the jj-th sample. When estimating the quantile P<yiP_{<y_{i}} for a current sample with reward R⁡(yi)R(y_{i}), we assign a decay weight wj=λ(T−tj)w_{j}=\lambda^{(T-t_{j})} to each historical sample, where TT is the current step and λ∈(0,1)\lambda\in(0,1) is a decay factor. The quantile is estimated via the weighted empirical CDF:

    P^<yi=∑(rj,tj)∈ℬwj⋅𝕀⁡(rj<R⁡(yi))∑(rj,tj)∈ℬwj\hat{P}_{<y_{i}}=\frac{\sum_{(r_{j},t_{j})\in\mathcal{B}}w_{j}\cdot\mathbb{I}(r_{j}<R(y_{i}))}{\sum_{(r_{j},t_{j})\in\mathcal{B}}w_{j}} (80)

    This effectively creates an exponential moving average of the distribution, ensuring the quantile reference remains synchronized with the current policy πθ\pi_{\theta}.

  • •

    For Majority Vote: We maintain an exponential moving average (EMA) of the consensus difficulty. If k^t\hat{k}_{t} is the ideal threshold estimated for batch tt, we update a global tracking variable k¯\bar{k} via k¯t+1=γ​k¯t+(1−γ)​k^t\bar{k}_{t+1}=\gamma\bar{k}_{t}+(1-\gamma)\hat{k}_{t}.

This technique allows us to estimate fine-grained global statistics required for the strategy-aware weights while keeping the active computational batch size MM small for efficiency.

B.8 Empirical Variance Reduction: Decoupling Utility from Step Size

A critical challenge in applying the strategy-aware gradient ∇θJCAT≈wi⋅∇θJBase\nabla_{\theta}J_{\text{CAT}}\approx w_{i}\cdot\nabla_{\theta}J_{\text{Base}} is the high variance of the weighting factor wiw_{i}. For instance, in Pass@NN, the raw marginal utility on "hard" prompts scales linearly with the budget (wi≈Nw_{i}\approx N). Directly applying these raw weights can result in extreme gradient magnitudes.

While it is theoretically correct that different prompts should command different gradient magnitudes, we must empirically bound the variance of the update step.

A naive approach to stabilization is prompt-level normalization, where weights are averaged within the MM rollouts of a single prompt xx: w^i=wi/𝔼⁡[w|x]\hat{w}_{i}=w_{i}/\mathbb{E}[w|x]. However, this is counterproductive. By forcing every prompt to exert an average gradient weight of 1, we inadvertently destroy the global capacity allocation mechanism, forcing the model to take full-sized gradient steps even on "solved" or "hopeless" prompts.

Instead, we employ Batch-Level Weight Normalization. For a global mini-batch BB containing multiple prompts and their respective rollouts, we normalize the strategy weights against the batch mean:

w~i=wi1|B|​∑j∈Bwj\tilde{w}_{i}=\frac{w_{i}}{\frac{1}{|B|}\sum_{j\in B}w_{j}} (81)

This rigorous formulation achieves two critical optimization goals simultaneously:

  1. 1.

    Step Size Stability: The expected magnitude of the CAT multiplier across the batch is exactly 1 (𝔼⁡[w~]=1\mathbb{E}[\tilde{w}]=1). This completely decouples the scale of the learning rate from the test-time budget NN, ensuring optimization stability regardless of the strategy used.

  2. 2.

    Preservation of Relative Capacity: Because the normalization factor is shared across all prompts in the batch, the relative weighting between different questions is perfectly preserved. A prompt at the Majority Vote "tipping point" will still exert proportionally more gradient pressure than a prompt that is safely solved, maintaining the core benefit of the strategy-aware objective.

B.9 On the Utilization of RL Rollouts for Exact Gradients

A natural extension to the diagonal approximation in the RL setting is to utilize the generated rollout batch to estimate the off-diagonal sensitivities ∂p~​(y∗|x)∂πθ​(y′|x)\frac{\partial\tilde{p}(y^{*}|x)}{\partial\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}|x)} for rival sequences. However, calculating this is highly non-trivial.

For aggregation strategies like Majority Vote, the sensitivity to a specific rival y′y^{\prime} depends on the probability that y′y^{\prime} dictates the consensus threshold. Evaluating this requires marginalizing over the joint distribution of all other possible outputs. Estimating these complex, multi-way dependencies from a sparse RL mini-batch (M≪NM\ll N) introduces extreme variance that destabilizes updates.

Rigorously handling these combinatorial credit-assignment dependencies without variance explosion is relegated to future work. In this work, we stick to the more robust, computationally efficient diagonal approximation.

Appendix C Extending to GRPO and PPO

While Appendix B derived the CAT gradients in the context of vanilla Policy Gradients (REINFORCE), modern LLM post-training relies on variance-reduced, trust-region methods such as Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) [] and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) [26].

Integrating the CAT into these algorithms requires careful handling of the advantage normalization step. We posit that the strategy-aware scaling factor must be treated as an external importance weight applied after the standard advantage estimation and normalization.

C.1 Strategy-Aware GRPO

GRPO eliminates the value function critic by using the group average reward as a baseline. For a prompt xx, GRPO samples a group of GG outputs {y1,…,yG}\{y_{1},\dots,y_{G}\} from the old policy πθo​l​d\pi_{\theta_{old}}.

Standard GRPO calculates the advantage AiA_{i} for the ii-th sample by normalizing the rewards within the group:

Ai=R⁡(yi)−mean​({R⁡(y1),…,R⁡(yG)})std​({R⁡(y1),…,R⁡(yG)})+ϵA_{i}=\frac{R(y_{i})-\text{mean}(\{R(y_{1}),\dots,R(y_{G})\})}{\text{std}(\{R(y_{1}),\dots,R(y_{G})\})+\epsilon} (82)

To align this with a test-time strategy 𝒯\mathcal{T}, we recall our core derivation: ∇JTTS≈wi⋅∇JBase\nabla J_{\text{TTS}}\approx w_{i}\cdot\nabla J_{\text{Base}}, where wi=∂p~∂piw_{i}=\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p_{i}} is the marginal utility of the sample under the strategy.

The Normalization Pitfall.

A naive approach might be to incorporate wiw_{i} directly into the reward, defining R~i=wi⋅R⁡(yi)\tilde{R}_{i}=w_{i}\cdot R(y_{i}). However, applying GRPO normalization to R~i\tilde{R}_{i} would be catastrophic. The normalization step (OPENR−μ)/σR-\mu)/\sigma is scale-invariant; it would cancel out the magnitude of wiw_{i}. For example, in Pass@NN, as the model approaches success, wi→0w_{i}\to 0. Normalization would rescale these vanishing rewards back to unit variance, effectively negating the efficiency regularization intended by the framework.

Correct Formulation.

We effectively treat the Test-Time strategy weight wiw_{i} as a sample-specific learning rate scaler. We compute the standard GRPO advantage AiA_{i} using the raw ground-truth rewards (or reward model scores), and apply wiw_{i} multiplicatively to the surrogate objective:

ℒGRPO-TTS(θ)=−1G∑i=1Gwi​(pi,ϕ)⏟CAT Weight⋅min(πθ​(yi|x)πθo​l​d​(yi|x)Ai,clip(…)Ai)\mathcal{L}_{\text{GRPO-TTS}}(\theta)=-\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\underbrace{w_{i}(p_{i},\phi)}_{\text{CAT Weight}}\cdot\min\left(\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{i}|x)}{\pi_{\theta_{old}}(y_{i}|x)}A_{i},\text{clip}(\dots)A_{i}\right) (83)

C.2 Implementation with PPO

The same logic applies to PPO [27] with a learned Value function Vψ​(x)V_{\psi}(x). We compute the Generalized Advantage Estimate (GAE) [28] A^t\hat{A}_{t} using the standard reward signal RtR_{t}. We then normalize the advantages across the batch: A^n​o​r​m=(A^−μ)/σ\hat{A}_{norm}=(\hat{A}-\mu)/\sigma.

The CAT weight is applied solely to the policy loss term:

ℒPPO-TTS=𝔼t​[wt⋅ℒtCLIP​(θ,A^n​o​r​m)−c1​ℒtVF−c2​S​[π]​(yt)]\mathcal{L}_{\text{PPO-TTS}}=\mathbb{E}_{t}\left[w_{t}\cdot\mathcal{L}^{\text{CLIP}}_{t}(\theta,\hat{A}_{norm})-c_{1}\mathcal{L}^{\text{VF}}_{t}-c_{2}S[\pi](y_{t})\right] (84)

By decoupling the strategy weight wtw_{t} from the advantage calculation, we ensure that the optimization landscape remains well-conditioned via normalization, while the gradient magnitude correctly reflects the sample’s contribution to the test-time metric.

Appendix D Interaction between CAT and RL Rollouts

A foundational premise of this work is that search and learning operate in a continuous, mutually beneficial cycle. A piece of this cycle that we have yet to touch on is, in the RL paradigm, how the altered CAT gradient affects how the model receives signals in future rollouts. We do not give a complete picture of that dynamic in this work but will use this section to discuss key observations.

A keen observer may have noticed a compelling anomaly in Section 3.2: the Pass@44 aligned model actually outperformed the baseline on single-shot accuracy (Pass@11). This is particularly noteworthy given that our training batch size was also 44. We hypothesize that by aligning the training objective with the generation budget, the model discovered a higher volume of correct reasoning paths during its rollouts, thereby enriching its own learning signal.

To test our hypothesis in a more controlled setting, we isolate the effect of strategy-aware SFT as a warmup phase for standard RL. In deep reinforcement learning for reasoning tasks, a primary bottleneck is sparse rewards: if the policy does not naturally generate the correct answer during its exploratory rollouts, it receives no positive reinforcement, leading to stalled learning. Standard SFT, which optimizes for single-sample precision, often exacerbates this by collapsing the generation variance and discouraging exploration, making it harder for the model to stumble upon the right reasoning path for difficult problems during the RL phase. Our goal is to use CAT to correct for this in the warmup.

Experimental Setup

To validate whether CAT can overcome this bottleneck, we trained one model using normal SFT and one model with Pass@16 CAT SFT for 1 epoch for 2000 samples following the same hyperparameters as our CAT SFT experiment in Section 3.1, followed by an epoch of GRPO on each model with a batch size of M=16M=16 and the same hyperparameters as in Appendix J. We then evaluated both models using the Pass@kk calculations from Appendix H across varying test-time budgets over 100 questions.

Results

As we can see in Table 9, the CAT model beat the normal SFT model at every single Test-Time metric, including Pass@1 after RL training.

Analysis

By applying CAT (Pass@1616) during the SFT warmup, we optimized the model for getting at least 1 answer right out of 16. When the CAT model transitions to the RL phase, it is more likely to get at least 1 of its 16 attempts per question right and receive signal. In this way, aligning the SFT warmup phase with a search strategy improves the sample efficiency and success rate of standard RL. We demonstrate that strategy-aware learning can actively improve the standard learning process itself. Here, CAT yields a more capable single-shot model (Pass@11).

However, to more broadly understand how CAT reshapes RL dynamics between successive rollouts, we must examine its effect on policy entropy. It is a well-established phenomenon that maintaining sufficient entropy is highly beneficial to robust RL training [29, 30], as it prevents premature mode collapse. While the precise evolutionary dynamics of the policy depend heavily on the specific TTS to which the RL is aligned, these modified objectives generally act to preserve policy entropy. By design, they penalize redundant overconfidence and instead maintain the distributional variance necessary to seed the search process effectively. This helps the model retain enough exploratory capacity during training to consistently allow the search strategy to discover and correct for the optimal answer. A more in-depth, specific analysis of these dynamics is saved for future work.

Appendix E Interpreting Scaling Factors

By visualizing the behavior of w⁡(p,ϕ)w(p,\phi), we can understand the mechanisms via which CAT works for each strategy.

E.1 Pass@NN: The Efficiency Regularizer

Pass@NN considers a prompt "solved" if any of the NN samples are correct.

As shown in Figures 12 and 12, the scaling factor for Pass@NN is monotonically decreasing with respect to the base model confidence pp.

  • •

    Diminishing Returns: For a standard model (N=1N=1), the gradient remains active even as p→1p\to 1, encouraging the model to memorize the sample. However, with N=64N=64 (Green line), the scaling factor collapses to near-zero once p≈0.1p\approx 0.1.

  • •

    Training Dynamics: This acts as an efficiency regularizer. The objective signals: "We are virtually guaranteed to find the answer within 64 tries; stop wasting capacity on this easy sample." This preserves model capacity for "hard" samples.

  • •

    Hard Example Boosting The RL weighing factor has one key property that the SFT factor does not which is that for p→0p\to 0, the RL factor boosts the gradient, optimizing for the tail of the distribution.

A deeper analysis of the SFT scaling factor (which is very similar to the RL factor) can be found in Chen et al. [8].

E.2 Majority Vote: The Tipping Point

Majority Vote requires the correct answer to achieve a plurality of the NN outputs. We reframe this as the requirement that the correct answer y∗y^{*} be selected at least kk times out of NN samples where k−1k-1 represents the number of times the most common incorrect answer gets chosen in the batch of NN.

SFT

As illustrated in Figure 14, the SFT scaling factor exhibits a monotonic decay, maximizing the gradient when p→0p\to 0.

When the base probability pp is small, the probability of achieving a majority p~\tilde{p} is exponentially small, resulting in a massive loss value. The scaling factor w≈kw\approx k acts as a "bootstrap" signal. It effectively forces the model to prioritize samples where it is currently failing, utilizing the ground truth to "pull" the probability mass toward the decision boundary regardless of the current policy distribution. Once the problem has already been "solved" as in it will likely win a plurality vote, the model learns to stop providing any gradient to it, since it doesn’t need to in order to get the problem right.

RL

In contrast, Reinforcement Learning (Figure 14) produces a "spotlight" centered on the decision boundary (p≈k/Np\approx k/N). It assigns near-zero weight to samples where the model is either "hopeless" (p≈0p\approx 0) or "secure" (p≈1p\approx 1).

Solving the Cold Start Problem.

The localized nature of the RL gradient creates a "cold start" vulnerability: if the model starts with p≈0p\approx 0, the gradient vanishes, and the model fails to learn.

As derived in Sec B.2, we resolve this not by altering the scaling curve, but by utilizing a dynamic threshold kk. In a specific batch, the threshold kk is determined by the strength of the rival answers. Early in training, when the model is weak, the threshold kk drops (e.g., to 10%10\%), shifting the gradient "spotlight" (The Red Curve in Figure 15) to overlap with the model’s current low-pp distribution. This allows the model to progressively "slide" the window of optimization from chaos to consensus. A similar logic provides rationale to iteratively increase the kk for SFT.

E.3 Best-of-NN: The Upper-Tail Optimizer

In the Best-of-NN setting, the system samples NN candidates and selects the single candidate with the maximum reward. While Best-of-NN for SFT reduces mathematically to Pass@NN (ensuring the ground truth appears once), in the Reinforcement Learning regime, the dynamics are distinct. The scaling factor, N​(P<y)N−1N(P_{<y})^{N-1}, depends not on absolute probability, but on the relative quantile of the reward distribution.

This shift from absolute probability to relative rank introduces three distinct behaviors:

1. Winner-Take-All Dynamics.

As visualized in Figure 16, the gradient weight vanishes for the bottom percentile of samples and explodes for the top percentile. The objective effectively ignores "average" performance. If a sample is not in the top quantile of the model’s potential outputs, it contributes zero signal. The model is only updated based on its best attempts, creating a "winner-take-all" feedback loop that aggressively reinforces the upper tail of the distribution.

2. Breaking Mode Collapse.

Standard objectives maximize expected utility. To minimize variance and maximize the average, these objectives encourage the model to collapse probability mass onto a single mode, usually a "safe," generic response. Diverging from this safe mode is typically penalized, as low-probability paths are treated as noise.

Best-of-NN inverts this incentive. By validating risky, low-density paths, the operator prevents the model from getting stuck at the local maxima of "safe" responses. It encourages the distribution to develop heavy tails, prioritizing the discovery of rare, high-reward solutions over the stability of the average output.

3. The "Safety Net" Effect.

Because the inference strategy acts as a filter, the model is not penalized for generating N−1N-1 failures, provided the NN-th sample succeeds. This effectively creates a safety net during training. The objective signals to the model: "You are allowed to fail N−1N-1 times, as long as your variance is high enough to produce one winner." This theoretically justifies training models that are less coherent on average, but significantly more capable at peak performance.

Appendix F Quantifying Misalignment

While the empirical results in Section 3 demonstrate that CAT improves performance, it is theoretically important to quantify when standard objectives fail. In this section, we formalize the disconnect between training and testing as a resource allocation problem. We introduce the Alignment Coefficient (𝒜\mathcal{A}) as a global metric for transfer efficiency. The general subject of seeing how optimizing for one loss may affect success on a different loss is deeply discussed in Gopalan et al. [31].

F.1 Derivation: The Alignment Coefficient (𝒜\mathcal{A})

To quantify the "transfer efficiency" of a training objective to a test-time metric, we analyze the impact of a single gradient descent step.

Let ℒtrain​(θ)\mathcal{L}_{\text{train}}(\theta) be the training loss we minimize, and 𝒰test​(θ)\mathcal{U}_{\text{test}}(\theta) be the test-time utility we wish to maximize. We perform a parameter update with learning rate η\eta:

θt+1=θt−η​∇θℒtrain\theta_{t+1}=\theta_{t}-\eta\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\text{train}} (85)

We are interested in the resulting change in the test utility, Δ​𝒰test=𝒰test​(θt+1)−𝒰test​(θt)\Delta\mathcal{U}_{\text{test}}=\mathcal{U}_{\text{test}}(\theta_{t+1})-\mathcal{U}_{\text{test}}(\theta_{t}). Applying a first-order Taylor expansion around θt\theta_{t}:

Δ​𝒰test\displaystyle\Delta\mathcal{U}_{\text{test}} ≈⟨∇θ𝒰test,(θt+1−θt)⟩\displaystyle\approx\langle\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{U}_{\text{test}},(\theta_{t+1}-\theta_{t})\rangle
=⟨∇θ𝒰test,−η​∇θℒtrain⟩\displaystyle=\langle\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{U}_{\text{test}},-\eta\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\text{train}}\rangle
=−η⁡⟨∇θ𝒰test,∇θℒtrain⟩\displaystyle=-\eta\langle\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{U}_{\text{test}},\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\text{train}}\rangle (86)

This result indicates that the immediate gain in test performance is proportional to the inner product of the training and test gradients.

As derived in Appendix A.1, for generative models, these gradients share the same directional component (the score function 𝐠=∇θ​log​πθ​(y|x)\mathbf{g}=\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y|x)) but differ in their scalar weighting functions w⁡(p)w(p):

∇ℒtrain\displaystyle\nabla\mathcal{L}_{\text{train}} =wtrain​(p)⋅𝐠\displaystyle=w_{\text{train}}(p)\cdot\mathbf{g} (87)
∇𝒰test\displaystyle\nabla\mathcal{U}_{\text{test}} =wtest​(p)⋅𝐠\displaystyle=w_{\text{test}}(p)\cdot\mathbf{g} (88)

Substituting this factorization into the inner product, we take the expectation over the data distribution p∼𝒟p\sim\mathcal{D}. In a rigorous setting, this expectation depends on the Empirical Confidence Density f𝒟​(p,θ)f_{\mathcal{D}}(p;\theta) (defined as the probability density function of the ground-truth likelihoods p⁡(y∗|x)p(y^{*}|x) across the dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D} given the current model parameters θ\theta), which shifts as the model matures.

𝔼[Δ𝒰test]∝−η∫01wtrain(p)wtest(p)⋅f𝒟(p;θ)⋅𝔼[∥𝐠∥2]dp\mathbb{E}[\Delta\mathcal{U}_{\text{test}}]\propto-\eta\int_{0}^{1}w_{\text{train}}(p)w_{\text{test}}(p)\cdot f_{\mathcal{D}}(p;\theta)\cdot\mathbb{E}[\|\mathbf{g}\|^{2}]\,dp (89)

While the true alignment is state-dependent, estimating f𝒟​(p)f_{\mathcal{D}}(p) requires tracking specific training dynamics. To derive a generalized metric, we assume p∼Unif​[0,1]p\sim\text{Unif}[0,1]. This acts as a trajectory average: since any successful model must traverse the probability space from ignorance (p≈0p\approx 0) to mastery (p≈1p\approx 1), integrating uniformly measures the alignment averaged over the entire lifecycle of training. This yields the Alignment Coefficient (𝒜\mathcal{A}):

𝒜⁡(Train,Test)=⟨wtrain,wtest⟩‖wtrain‖2⋅‖wtest‖2=∫01wtrain​(p)​wtest​(p)​𝑑p∫01wtrain2​(p)​𝑑p​∫01wtest2​(p)​𝑑p\mathcal{A}(\text{Train},\text{Test})=\frac{\langle w_{\text{train}},w_{\text{test}}\rangle}{\|w_{\text{train}}\|_{2}\cdot\|w_{\text{test}}\|_{2}}=\frac{\int_{0}^{1}w_{\text{train}}(p)w_{\text{test}}(p)\,dp}{\sqrt{\int_{0}^{1}w_{\text{train}}^{2}(p)\,dp}\sqrt{\int_{0}^{1}w_{\text{test}}^{2}(p)\,dp}} (90)

This metric provides a normalized scalar 𝒜∈[0,1]\mathcal{A}\in[0,1]. By decoupling the objective function from the data distribution, 𝒜\mathcal{A} allows us to measure the intrinsic compatibility of the training loss with the test metric, independent of the model’s current calibration.

  • •

    𝒜≈1\mathcal{A}\approx 1 (Perfect Alignment): The training objective applies gradient pressure exactly where the test metric demands it, maximizing Δ​𝒰test\Delta\mathcal{U}_{\text{test}} regardless of data density.

  • •

    𝒜≈0\mathcal{A}\approx 0 (Orthogonality): The training objective is active in regions where the test metric has zero utility. In this case, Δ​𝒰test≈0\Delta\mathcal{U}_{\text{test}}\approx 0, meaning the training compute is inherently wasted relative to the target task.

F.2 Physical Interpretation: Gradient Misallocation

Why should we care about the abstract scalar 𝒜\mathcal{A}? Because it serves as a rigorous proxy for Gradient Misallocation.

Neural network training is a zero-sum game of resource allocation. The "resource" is the finite gradient magnitude the model can absorb before convergence. We define the Effective Support of an objective as the region 𝒮={p∣w⁡(p)>ϵ}\mathcal{S}=\{p\mid w(p)>\epsilon\}. Misalignment occurs when the supports of wtrainw_{\text{train}} and wtestw_{\text{test}} are disjoint.

As illustrated in Figure 17, we can decompose the probability space into three regions:

  1. 1.

    The Efficient Region (𝒮overlap\mathcal{S}_{\text{overlap}}): Where both objectives are active.

  2. 2.

    The Waste Region (Ωwaste\Omega_{\text{waste}}): Where the training objective applies pressure, but the test metric is already satiated (wtest≈0w_{\text{test}}\approx 0). Gradients here are "wasted" on perfecting samples that are already good enough.

  3. 3.

    The Starvation Region (Ωstarve\Omega_{\text{starve}}): Where the test metric demands improvement (wtest>0w_{\text{test}}>0), but the training objective provides no signal (wtrain≈0w_{\text{train}}\approx 0).

The Alignment Coefficient 𝒜\mathcal{A} is mathematically dominated by the integral over the overlap 𝒮overlap\mathcal{S}_{\text{overlap}}. Therefore, a low 𝒜\mathcal{A} guarantees high gradient misallocation. It allows us to detect inefficiency without needing to define arbitrary "satiation thresholds" for every metric.

F.3 Transfer Analysis

Finally, we can use the Alignment Coefficient to answer a practical question: How much does training for hyperparameters ϕt​r​a​i​n\phi_{train} improve performance at a different inference hyperparameter ϕt​e​s​t\phi_{test}? We stick to the Pass@NN case for this subsection where ϕt​r​a​i​n=Nt​r​a​i​n\phi_{train}=N_{train} and ϕt​e​s​t=Nt​e​s​t\phi_{test}=N_{test}. The coefficient allows us to analytically predict the test-time budget Nt​e​s​tN_{test} where a model trained for a larger budget NBN_{B} will overtake a model trained for a smaller budget NAN_{A}. We find this theoretical crossover point by setting their alignment coefficients equal to each other:

𝒜⁡(NA,Nt​e​s​t)=𝒜⁡(NB,Nt​e​s​t)\mathcal{A}(N_{A},N_{test})=\mathcal{A}(N_{B},N_{test}) (91)

To empirically validate this framework, we numerically integrated the Alignment Coefficients for the Pass@NN SFT objective across our experimental training budgets Ntrain∈{1,4,16,64}N_{\text{train}}\in\{1,4,16,64\} against a continuous spectrum of inference budgets Ntest∈[1,64]N_{\text{test}}\in[1,64]. By tracking the trajectory of these coefficients, we can identify the exact theoretical crossover points where 𝒜⁡(Nlarger,Ntest)>𝒜⁡(Nsmaller,Ntest)\mathcal{A}(N_{\text{larger}},N_{\text{test}})>\mathcal{A}(N_{\text{smaller}},N_{\text{test}}).

This numerical evaluation yields three specific predictions for when a larger training budget should overtake a smaller one:

  1. 1.

    N=4N=4 overtakes the baseline (N=1N=1) at Ntest=2N_{\text{test}}=2, where the alignment coefficient for N=4N=4 reaches 0.92950.9295 compared to 0.91000.9100 for the baseline.

  2. 2.

    N=16N=16 overtakes N=4N=4 at Ntest=8N_{\text{test}}=8, with an alignment score of 0.93410.9341 edging out 0.93320.9332.

  3. 3.

    N=64N=64 overtakes N=16N=16 at Ntest=32N_{\text{test}}=32, achieving a coefficient of 0.93440.9344 against 0.93430.9343.

These theoretical predictions align remarkably well with the empirical observations from the MATH benchmark (Table 2, Figure 1).

First, the baseline model dominates at Pass@1, but the N=4N=4 model catches up around Pass@2. This bounds the first crossover exactly where the theory places it (Ntest=2N_{\text{test}}=2).

Next, the theoretical framework predicts that the N=16N=16 model will overtake the N=4N=4 model exactly at Ntest=8N_{\text{test}}=8. Looking at our empirical data, Pass@8 is just around the budget where the N=16N=16 model (40.33%40.33\%) eclipses the N=4N=4 model (39.87%39.87\%).

Finally, the framework predicts N=64N=64 will overtake N=16N=16 at Ntest=32N_{\text{test}}=32. Empirically, at Pass@32, the two models are neck-and-neck (59.29%59.29\% vs 59.85%59.85\%), representing the exact empirical threshold of the crossover before the N=64N=64 model pulls definitively ahead by Pass@64 (67.60%67.60\% vs 66.20%66.20\%).

This tight correspondence between the purely theoretical Alignment Coefficient and the observed scaling laws demonstrates that 𝒜⁡(Train,Test)\mathcal{A}(\text{Train},\text{Test}) can be used as a cheap predictive tool to match training hyperparameters to an expected deployment budget without relying on expensive empirical sweeps.

Appendix G Why Not Just Perform Full TTS Rollouts?

A seemingly intuitive alternative to the CAT framework is to simply simulate the TTS exactly during the RL phase. For instance, to train for Pass@NN, one could generate NN full rollouts per prompt, compute the empirical aggregate reward (e.g., 11 if any of the NN samples are correct, 00 otherwise), and use this as the reinforcement signal. With a leave-one-out baseline to stabilize the variance of this strategy, this is what Tang et al. [11] do in their work. While conceptually straightforward and more effective than standard training in this context, this empirical rollout approach suffers from two fatal flaws: computational inflexibility and credit assignment.

G.1 The Computational Bottleneck: Inflexibility of Batch Size

The most immediate barrier to empirical TTS rollouts is the strict coupling of the training compute budget to the target inference budget. If the target deployment strategy is Pass@6464 or Majority Vote over 128 samples, an empirical training objective requires generating exactly N=64N=64 or N=128N=128 complete trajectories for every single prompt in the training batch.

This O⁡(N)O(N) scaling of generation cost per step creates a severe computational bottleneck. It drastically limits the number of unique prompts the model can see per epoch with fixed compute, restricting dataset coverage. In contrast, CAT completely decouples the training rollout budget (MM) from the target inference budget (NN). By using the analytical derivative of the effective probability ∂p~∂p\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p}, CAT can train a model for Pass@100100 while only generating M=4M=4 rollouts per prompt during training, resulting in massive efficiency gains.

G.2 Credit Assignment: Learning Signal Degeneracy

The second, more insidious issue with full TTS rollouts is the mathematical degeneracy of the learning signal when dealing with aggregate rewards and the inability to assign credit to specific outputs.

Consider the empirical Pass@NN objective, where the aggregate reward for a batch of NN generations is simply the global maximum of the individual binary rewards: Rbatch=max⁡(r1,…,rN)R_{\text{batch}}=\max(r_{1},\dots,r_{N}). In a standard RL setup (e.g., REINFORCE with a leave-one-out baseline like in Tang et al. [11]), the advantage AiA_{i} for a specific sample yiy_{i} is the difference between the global aggregate reward and the aggregate reward excluding yiy_{i}. Mathematically, this is expressed as:

Ai=max(r1:N)−max(r−i)A_{i}=\max(r_{1:N})-\max(r_{-i})

This formulation reveals a critical flaw. Imagine we are training for Pass@6464, and the model generates 3 correct answers out of the 64 rollouts. The global maximum reward is 11. If we evaluate the advantage for any of the 3 correct answers by "leaving it out," the remaining batch still contains 2 correct answers. Therefore, the leave-one-out maximum is still 11. The advantage calculation becomes:

Ai=1−1=0A_{i}=1-1=0

If the model solves the problem more than once in the batch, the advantage for every single sample zeroes out. The model receives no learning signal if it gets 3 correct instead of 2 correct, or 64 correct instead of 2 correct. As NN scales, the probability of this issue coming into play scales, meaning information is wasted.

CAT avoids this degeneracy entirely. Instead of relying on a discrete empirical step-function, CAT operates on the continuous, analytical gradient of the expected test-time probability. Even if the empirical batch is saturated with correct answers, the scalar weight w⁡(p,ϕ)w(p,\phi) evaluates the underlying probability mass pp. This ensures a smooth, continuous gradient that always accurately reflects the marginal utility of shifting the probability distribution, preventing the signal from vanishing.

Appendix H Experimental Details: Pass@NN SFT

This and all other experiments were run on an Nvidia V100 GPU on a cluster with around 20 Gigabytes of storage.

H.1 Hyperparameters and Training Configuration

All models were initialized from Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 (4-bit quantized) and fine-tuned using the Unsloth library [32]. We utilized a global effective batch size of 4 (real batch size 1 with 4 gradient accumulation steps). The specific hyperparameters are detailed in Table 10.

H.2 Pass@NN Implementation

Loss Computation.

Directly computing Pass@NN loss via probabilities p=exp⁡(logits)p=\exp(\text{logits}) leads to floating-point underflow when p→0p\to 0. To address this, our implementation operates primarily in log-space and includes a branch for low-probability events.

Let ℓseq\ell_{\text{seq}} be the sequence-level negative log-likelihood. The base probability is p=exp⁡(−ℓseq)p=\exp(-\ell_{\text{seq}}). The loss is defined as:

ℒPass​@​N={ℓseq−log⁡(N)if ​p<10−4−log⁡(1−(1−p)N)otherwise\mathcal{L}_{\text{Pass}@N}=\begin{cases}\ell_{\text{seq}}-\log(N)&\text{if }p<10^{-4}\\ -\log\left(1-(1-p)^{N}\right)&\text{otherwise}\end{cases} (92)

For the "tiny" probability regime (p<10−4p<10^{-4}), we approximate Pass@N≈N​pN\approx Np. Maximizing log⁡(N​p)\log(Np) is equivalent to minimizing −log⁡p−log⁡N-\log p-\log N. This linear approximation prevents gradient collapse when the model is far from the solution manifold.

Evaluation.

We evaluated the models by generating a fixed pool of K=64K=64 samples per problem. To efficiently estimate Pass@kk for varying budgets k≤64k\leq 64 without resampling, we utilized the unbiased estimator for selection without replacement:

Pass​@​k=1−∏i=0k−1n−c−in−i\text{Pass}@k=1-\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}\frac{n-c-i}{n-i} (93)

where n=64n=64 is the pool size and cc is the count of correct samples.

Appendix I Majority Vote SFT Implementation Details

This and all other experiments were run on an Nvidia V100 GPU on a cluster with around 20 Gigabytes of storage.

I.1 Training Configuration and Data Processing

Similar to the Pass@NN experiments, models trained for Majority Vote were initialized from Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 (4-bit quantized) and fine-tuned using the Unsloth library. The optimization hyperparameters (learning rate, batch size, etc.) follow the standard configuration detailed in Table 10. We used the Peft [33] and Transformers [34] libraries as backbones for our experiments.

Crucially, because Majority Vote requires the model to have a non-trivial baseline success rate to form a meaningful consensus, the training and testing subsets of the MATH dataset were filtered to include only difficulty levels 1 through 3. This ensures that the base probability pp is sufficiently far from zero, preserving numerical stability during gradient scaling and providing a dense enough signal for plurality dynamics to take effect.

I.2 Implicit Log-Space Loss Computation

Directly computing the effective probability p~\tilde{p} for Majority Vote involves summing binomial coefficients: p~=∑i=kN(Ni)​pi​(1−p)N−i\tilde{p}=\sum_{i=k}^{N}\binom{N}{i}p^{i}(1-p)^{N-i}. This naive calculation leads to severe numerical instability, specifically underflow when probabilities are small, or overflow when NN is large.

To resolve this, our implementation calculates the loss strictly in log-space using a Log-Sum-Exp reduction. For a given input sequence, we compute the per-token negative log-likelihood (NLL) via standard Cross-Entropy, ignoring padding tokens. Summing these yields the sequence-level NLL, ℓseq\ell_{\text{seq}}, from which we derive the base probability p=exp⁡(−ℓseq)p=\exp(-\ell_{\text{seq}}). To ensure stability during training, pp is tightly clamped to the interval [10−6,1−10−6][10^{-6},1-10^{-6}].

Let ff be the target consensus fraction k/Nk/N (e.g., 0.50.5 for simple majority). The absolute token threshold is dynamically computed as k=max⁡(2,min⁡(N,⌈N⋅f⌉))k=\max(2,\min(N,\lceil N\cdot f\rceil)). We iterate through each possible winning vote count i∈[k,N]i\in[k,N] and compute the log-probability of that specific outcome using the log⁡Γ\log\Gamma function to continuously approximate the combinations:

log⁡Ti=log⁡Γ⁡(N+1)−log⁡Γ⁡(i+1)−log⁡Γ⁡(N−i+1)+i​log⁡(p)+(N−i)​log⁡(1−p)\log T_{i}=\log\Gamma(N+1)-\log\Gamma(i+1)-\log\Gamma(N-i+1)+i\log(p)+(N-i)\log(1-p) (94)

The final success log-probability is aggregated using the Log-Sum-Exp trick over all valid ii:

log⁡p~=LogSumExp​(log⁡Tk,…,log⁡TN)\log\tilde{p}=\text{LogSumExp}(\log T_{k},\dots,\log T_{N}) (95)

The computed log⁡p~\log\tilde{p} is then negated and normalized by the number of valid tokens in the target sequence to form the final strategy-aware loss.

I.3 Evaluation via Bootstrapped Sampling

Unlike Pass@NN, which benefits from a simple unbiased estimator for test-time scaling, Majority Vote requires aggregating across the plurality of competing answers. Running exact combinatorial evaluations across large sets is computationally prohibitive.

To accurately estimate Majority Vote accuracy across varying inference budgets (up to k=128k=128), we employed a highly smoothed Monte Carlo bootstrapping approach. For each problem in the test set, we generated a pool of 128 candidate responses using a sampling temperature of 0.80.8 and Top-pp of 0.950.95.

To evaluate the model at a specific inference budget kk, we ran 500 bootstrap iterations per problem. In each iteration, we sampled kk responses from the generated pool without replacement. The textual answers were parsed, and the most common valid answer (the mode) was selected as the system’s final output. The overall Maj@kk performance is reported as the empirical win rate of this system output averaged across all 500 iterations and all test problems.

I.4 Hyperparameter Sensitivity (The Sweep)

For the Majority Vote objective, the consensus threshold fraction ff is a critical hyperparameter. If ff is too low, the objective is trivial; if ff is too high, the gradient vanishes because the consensus is mathematically unreachable from the current policy. We performed a grid search over consensus fractions f∈{0.25,0.33,0.40}f\in\{0.25,0.33,0.40\} for the different budgets, below we include an example in Figure 18.

As shown in Figure 18, the model is highly sensitive to this threshold. The model trained with f=0.25f=0.25 (requiring only 16/64 votes) actually degraded performance (AUC −0.1-0.1). We interpret this as a "weak signal" failure mode: the constraint was so loose that the model could satisfy it with a high-entropy distribution, rather than being forced to converge on the ground truth. Increasing the requirement to f=0.40f=0.40 (26/64 votes) provided the necessary "pressure" to guide the model toward a robust consensus. For the Maj@88 model f=.33f=.33 won out and for the Maj@1616 model f=.25f=.25 won out.

Appendix J Pass@NN Reinforcement Learning Implementation Details

This and all other experiments were run on an Nvidia V100 GPU on a cluster with around 20 Gigabytes of storage.

J.1 Training Configuration and Data Processing

For the Reinforcement Learning experiments, we initialized the policy from a checkpoint that had already undergone a Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) warmup. This warmup establishes a baseline capability for formatting mathematical reasoning traces and extracting final answers.

We utilized the trl library’s [35] Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) trainer, wrapped with our custom strategy-aware weighting logic, and fine-tuned using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) [36] on the 4-bit quantized [37] Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 model. We use the AdamW [38] optimizer. A critical detail of our GRPO setup is the group size (number of generations per prompt), which we set to G=4G=4 to balance variance reduction with memory constraints. The full optimization hyperparameters are detailed in Table 11.

J.2 Reward Formulation

Because Pass@NN evaluates the ultimate correctness of a generation rather than the intermediate steps, we employed a binary, outcome-based reward function. For a generated sequence yy, we extract the final answer (either via LaTeX \boxed{} tags or trailing numerics) and compare it against the ground truth. The raw reward is R⁡(y)=1.0R(y)=1.0 for a correct match and R⁡(y)=0.0R(y)=0.0 otherwise. GRPO internally normalizes these raw rewards within the sampled group of size G=4G=4 to compute the baseline advantage AiA_{i} for each sequence.

J.3 Log-Weighted Advantage Scaling (The Core Logic)

To adapt GRPO for Pass@NN, we modify the objective by applying a sample-specific scaling factor wiw_{i} to the computed advantage AiA_{i}. Our primary implementation uses the "Log-Weighted" formulation (derived from the SFT objective in Section A.2), which includes an adaptive gain controller to stabilize the variance of the RL updates.

Estimating the Sequence Probability (pp).

To compute the scaling factor, we require the model’s base likelihood of generating the current sequence yiy_{i}. During the forward pass, we extract the log-softmax distribution over the vocabulary and gather the log-probabilities of the actual generated tokens. We mask out the prompt tokens and sum the completion token log-probabilities to yield the raw sequence log-probability, ℓseq\ell_{\text{seq}}.

Because raw sequence probabilities in LLMs can vanish to infinitesimally small values, directly exponentiating ℓseq\ell_{\text{seq}} often results in a floating-point underflow to 0.00.0. To maintain a usable gradient signal, we aggressively clamp the sequence log-probability before exponentiation:

pi=exp⁡(clamp​(ℓseq,−50.0,0.0))p_{i}=\exp(\text{clamp}(\ell_{\text{seq}},-50.0,0.0)) (96)

This establishes a strict numerical floor, ensuring pip_{i} does not drop below ≈1.9×10−22\approx 1.9\times 10^{-22}. For further stability during division, pip_{i} is subsequently clamped to the interval [10−10,1−10−10][10^{-10},1-10^{-10}].

Computing the Stabilized Weight (wiw_{i}).

The Log-Weighted scaling factor incorporates the raw marginal utility and the p/p~p/\tilde{p} normalization term. To prevent overflow when NN is large or pp is small, we compute the numerator in log-space:

Numerator=exp⁡(log⁡(N)+log⁡(pi)+(N−1)​log⁡(1−pi))\text{Numerator}=\exp\Big(\log(N)+\log(p_{i})+(N-1)\log(1-p_{i})\Big) (97)

The denominator represents the effective test-time probability p~\tilde{p}, computed as 1−(1−pi)N1-(1-p_{i})^{N}. The final weight is wi=Numerator/(p~+10−10)w_{i}=\text{Numerator}/(\tilde{p}+10^{-10}).

Gradient Weight Clipping.

Even with the log-weighted formulation acting as an adaptive gain controller, batches containing exceptionally "hard" examples can occasionally produce large scaling factors. To definitively prevent variance explosion and policy destabilization, we apply a hard clipping ceiling to the final weight:

wi=clamp​(wi,0.0,50.0)w_{i}=\text{clamp}(w_{i},0.0,50.0) (98)

The final strategy-aware loss for the sample becomes ℒi=−(wi⋅Ai)⋅ℓseq\mathcal{L}_{i}=-(w_{i}\cdot A_{i})\cdot\ell_{\text{seq}}, effectively scaling the learning rate of the specific sequence proportional to its marginal utility under the Pass@NN metric.

J.4 Test-Time Evaluation

To evaluate the scaling laws of the trained RL models, we evaluated them on a held-out set of 150 MATH problems. For each prompt, we generated K=32K=32 independent solutions using a sampling temperature of 0.70.7 and Top-pp of 0.90.9.

We computed the Pass@kk performance at inference budgets k∈{1,…,32}k\in\{1,\dots,32\} using the unbiased estimator for selection without replacement. Specifically, if cc is the total number of correct answers found in the KK generations, the expected Pass@kk score is:

Pass​@​k=1−∏i=0k−1(1−cK−i)\text{Pass}@k=1-\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}\left(1-\frac{c}{K-i}\right) (99)

This allows us to construct smooth, variance-reduced scaling curves across varying inference budgets without needing to repeatedly resample from the model.

Appendix K Majority Vote RL Implementation Details

This and all other experiments were run on an Nvidia V100 GPU on a cluster with around 20 Gigabytes of storage.

K.1 Pipeline Configuration

We utilized the Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 model as our policy πθ\pi_{\theta}. To manage memory constraints on consumer-grade hardware, we employed QLoRA (4-bit quantization with NF4 data type) via the bitsandbytes library [39]. The policy was trained using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) with rank r=16r=16 and α=32\alpha=32, targeting the q_proj and v_proj modules.

The training pipeline consisted of two phases:

  1. 1.

    SFT Warmup: The model was first fine-tuned for 3 epochs on the target dataset (MATH levels 1–3) using standard Cross-Entropy loss. This phase stabilizes the instruction-following capabilities and ensures the model outputs valid reasoning traces.

  2. 2.

    Strategy-Aware RL: The warmed-up model was then trained for 1 epoch using our custom weighted gradient estimator.

K.2 Dynamic Consensus Thresholding

A critical challenge in optimizing for Majority Vote is determining the required consensus threshold kk during training. While at test time kk is fixed (e.g., ⌊N/2⌋+1\lfloor N/2\rfloor+1), during training with small batch sizes (rollouts), the "strength" of the rival answers fluctuates.

We implemented an Adaptive kk Scaling mechanism. For a target inference budget Nt​a​r​g​e​tN_{target} (e.g., 4 or 8) and a training rollout size MM (set to 8 in our experiments), we project the difficulty of the current prompt to the target budget.

Let cm​a​xc_{max} be the count of the most frequent incorrect answer in the current rollout of size MM. The projected number of adversary votes in the target budget Nt​a​r​g​e​tN_{target} is:

E⁡[wrong]=cm​a​x×Nt​a​r​g​e​tME[\text{wrong}]=c_{max}\times\frac{N_{target}}{M} (100)

The required consensus kd​y​n​a​m​i​ck_{dynamic} is strictly one vote greater than the projected adversary:

kd​y​n​a​m​i​c=⌊E⁡[wrong]⌋+1k_{dynamic}=\lfloor E[\text{wrong}]\rfloor+1 (101)

We clamp this value such that 2≤kd​y​n​a​m​i​c≤⌊Nt​a​r​g​e​t/2⌋+12\leq k_{dynamic}\leq\lfloor N_{target}/2\rfloor+1. This ensures that the gradient "spotlight" (the weighting factor) focuses on the margin of victory required to beat the specific rival present in the current generation, rather than a static vacuum.

K.3 Advantage Computation and Zero-Mean Penalty

We utilized a simplified Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) framework. For each prompt xx, we generated M=8M=8 rollouts. The binary rewards ri∈{0,1}r_{i}\in\{0,1\} were normalized to compute advantages AiA_{i}:

Ai=ri−μrσr+ϵA_{i}=\frac{r_{i}-\mu_{r}}{\sigma_{r}+\epsilon} (102)

The Silence Penalty: A common failure mode in reasoning-heavy RL is "total collapse," where all MM rollouts are incorrect (μr=0\mu_{r}=0). Standard normalization would result in Ai=0A_{i}=0 (undefined gradient). To explicitly penalize this state and force exploration, we implemented a shift:

if ​μr=0,Ai←Ai−0.5\text{if }\mu_{r}=0,\quad A_{i}\leftarrow A_{i}-0.5 (103)

This ensures that if the model produces a batch of pure failures, it receives a negative reinforcement signal, pushing the policy away from the current mode.

K.4 Hyperparameters

Table 12 lists the exact hyperparameters used in the experiments. The learning rate for the RL phase was significantly lower than the SFT phase (1×10−61\times 10^{-6}) to prevent policy collapse given the high variance of the weighting factors.

Appendix L Best-of-NN RL Implementation: Unconditional Protein Generation

This and all other experiments were run on an Nvidia V100 GPU on a cluster with around 20 Gigabytes of storage.

L.1 Training Configuration and Biochemical Topology

For the unconditional protein generation task, we initialized the policy using the pre-trained nferruz/ProtGPT2 model (738M parameters). The objective of this experiment was to test the model’s ability to traverse a multi-modal reward landscape (the "Valley of Death") to discover a rare, high-reward global optimum.

While this reward landscape is mathematically engineered to test optimization dynamics, it abstracts a fundamental thermodynamic challenge in protein engineering: the design of stable transmembrane domains without triggering aggregation. Let h⁡(y)h(y) represent the hydrophobicity ratio of a generated sequence yy, defined as the fraction of amino acids belonging to the hydrophobic set {A, I, L, M, F, W, Y, V}. The reward function explicitly models three biochemical states:

R⁡(y)=4.0​exp⁡(−(h⁡(y)−0.35)20.05)+12.0​exp⁡(−(h⁡(y)−0.75)20.015)+Penalty​(y)R(y)=4.0\exp\left(-\frac{(h(y)-0.35)^{2}}{0.05}\right)+12.0\exp\left(-\frac{(h(y)-0.75)^{2}}{0.015}\right)+\text{Penalty}(y) (104)
  • •

    The Trap (h≈0.35h\approx 0.35): This represents standard, water-soluble globular proteins. Because the vast majority of characterized proteins in the pre-training data are soluble, the language model naturally gravitates here. It acts as a highly stable, "safe" local optimum.

  • •

    The Jackpot (h≈0.75h\approx 0.75): This represents highly hydrophobic integral membrane proteins. These sequences are extremely valuable as therapeutic targets (e.g., GPCRs) but are structurally narrow and generationally rare.

  • •

    The Valley (0.45<h<0.600.45<h<0.60): Intermediate hydrophobicity creates "sticky" sequences. They possess too many exposed hydrophobic patches to remain soluble in water, but lack the uniform hydrophobicity required to stably insert into a lipid bilayer. Biologically, these sequences misfold and form toxic aggregates (e.g., amyloid fibrils). We model this by applying Penalty​(y)=−2.0\text{Penalty}(y)=-2.0 if the sequence falls into this aggregation zone.

Standard RL gets stuck in the soluble "Trap" because moving toward the transmembrane "Jackpot" requires traversing the heavily penalized aggregation "Valley." To prevent the model from generating pathologically short sequences or non-biological repetitions to game the metric, any sequence shorter than 10 amino acids receives a flat reward of −5.0-5.0, and the RL objective includes a Kullback-Leibler divergence penalty (β=0.3\beta=0.3) [40] against the frozen pre-trained reference model. The model was trained for 300 steps with a learning rate of 1×10−51\times 10^{-5}.

L.2 Global Quantile Estimation for Best-of-NN

The Best-of-NN RL objective relies on weighting the policy gradient by the marginal utility of the sample under a search process, which we derived as proportional to N​(P<y)N−1N(P_{<y})^{N-1}. The critical parameter to estimate is P<yP_{<y}, the probability that a random sample from the current policy yields a reward strictly lower than the current sequence yy.

Because the unconditional reward landscape is static (the reward depends solely on the output sequence), we can accurately estimate this quantile using a global historical buffer. Relying strictly on small in-batch ranks introduces excessive variance; a mediocre sample might appear excellent simply because the rest of the batch was exceptionally poor.

We maintain a global, rolling First-In-First-Out (FIFO) buffer ℬ\mathcal{B} containing the rewards of the most recent 4,000 generated sequences. For a newly generated sequence yiy_{i} with reward RiR_{i}, its global quantile is estimated as the fraction of historical samples it outperforms, smoothed to prevent zero-probabilities:

P<yi=clamp​(∑r∈ℬ𝕀⁡(r<Ri)+1|ℬ|+2, 0.001, 0.999)P_{<y_{i}}=\text{clamp}\left(\frac{\sum_{r\in\mathcal{B}}\mathbb{I}(r<R_{i})+1}{|\mathcal{B}|+2},\;0.001,\;0.999\right) (105)

L.3 Gradient Weight Normalization

The raw Best-of-NN scaling weight is computed as wi=N​(P<yi)N−1w_{i}=N(P_{<y_{i}})^{N-1}. Because this function is highly convex (exponentially decaying for all but the top percentile), applying it directly alters the effective magnitude of the overall gradient step, which can stall training if the entire batch falls into a low-quantile regime.

To decouple the direction of the update from the magnitude of the learning rate, we normalize the weights across the current batch MM:

w~i=wi1M​∑j=1Mwj\tilde{w}_{i}=\frac{w_{i}}{\frac{1}{M}\sum_{j=1}^{M}w_{j}} (106)

This batch-level normalization ensures that the expected scale of the gradient remains consistent with standard RL, while strictly redistributing the optimization capacity toward the highest-performing samples in the batch. The final normalized weight w~i\tilde{w}_{i} is detached from the computation graph and multiplied by the standard normalized advantage to compute the loss.

Appendix M Best-of-NN RL Implementation: Conditional Protein Generation

This and all other experiments were run on an Nvidia V100 GPU on a cluster with around 20 Gigabytes of storage.

M.1 Dataset Formulation and Biochemical Motivation

The conditional generation experiment tests the framework’s ability to learn complex relational rules. We synthesized a PairedProteinDataset where each prompt contains an input sequence with a specific hydrophobicity hi​nh_{in}. The task is to generate an output sequence satisfying the inverse rule: ht​a​r​g​e​t=1.0−hi​nh_{target}=1.0-h_{in}.

This inverse relationship abstracts a critical practical objective in biomolecular engineering: the design of compensatory fusion tags and amphiphilic binding partners. For instance, researchers frequently need to append highly hydrophilic sequences (e.g., SUMO or GST tags, h≈0.2h\approx 0.2) to forcibly solubilize highly hydrophobic target proteins (h≈0.8h\approx 0.8) for crystallization or manufacturing. Conversely, a highly hydrophilic catalytic domain might require the fusion of a hydrophobic anchor to ensure localization to a cellular membrane.

To ground the generation process, the model underwent a Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) warmup phase. We generated 2,000 "gold" pairs where the target sequences were explicitly constructed to perfectly satisfy the compensatory relationship. The base ProtGPT2 model was fine-tuned on this dataset for 60 steps at a learning rate of 5×10−65\times 10^{-6} using standard cross-entropy, establishing a functional prior for the subsequent RL phase.

M.2 Relational Reward and Penalty

During the RL phase, the reward function dynamically evaluates the generated tag’s thermodynamic complementarity to the input sequence. For an input hydrophobicity hi​nh_{in} and generated output yy, the reward is defined as a Gaussian ridge centered on the inverse target:

R⁡(y,hi​n)=10.0​exp⁡(−(h⁡(y)−(1−hi​n))20.05)+Penalty​(y,hi​n)R(y,h_{in})=10.0\exp\left(-\frac{(h(y)-(1-h_{in}))^{2}}{0.05}\right)+\text{Penalty}(y,h_{in}) (107)

To prevent the model from discovering a trivial "identity mapping" shortcut (i.e., simply copying the input sequence, which yields deceptively high rewards for inputs near hi​n≈0.5h_{in}\approx 0.5), we explicitly penalize the model. A penalty of −2.0-2.0 is applied if the output hydrophobicity matches the input (|h⁡(y)−hi​n|<0.1|h(y)-h_{in}|<0.1) AND the input is sufficiently far from the midpoint (|hi​n−0.5|>0.1|h_{in}-0.5|>0.1). This constraint forces the model to genuinely learn sequence complementarity rather than sequence repetition.

The RL optimization utilized a batch size of 25, a learning rate of 2×10−62\times 10^{-6}, and a lower KL penalty (β=0.05\beta=0.05) to allow the model more flexibility to diverge from the SFT prior.

M.3 In-Batch Rank Estimation (Dynamic Quantiles)

Unlike the unconditional task, the reward landscape in the conditional task shifts dynamically with every prompt. An absolute reward of 5.05.0 might represent a spectacular success for a highly complex input sequence, but a mediocre failure for an easy one. Consequently, evaluating a sequence against a global historical buffer of rewards (which aggregates across differing inputs) would yield a mathematically invalid quantile P<yP_{<y}.

Therefore, for conditional Best-of-NN RL, we exclusively utilize in-batch rank estimation. Because all generated sequences in a specific mini-batch are conditioned on the same inputs, their rewards are directly comparable.
