For a batch of MM generated sequences (in our implementation, M=25M=25), we sort the rewards and assign an ascending integer rank to each sample (where 00 is the worst and M−1M-1 is the best). The empirical quantile is computed smoothly as:

P<yi=rank​(Ri)+1M+1P_{<y_{i}}=\frac{\text{rank}(R_{i})+1}{M+1} (108)

This ensures that the Best-of-NN weight wi=N​(P<yi)N−1w_{i}=N(P_{<y_{i}})^{N-1} accurately reflects the relative success of a sequence conditioned specifically on its prompt. As with the unconditional formulation, these weights are batch-normalized (w~i=wi/𝔼⁡[w]\tilde{w}_{i}=w_{i}/\mathbb{E}[w]) before being applied to the advantage scaled log-probabilities.

Appendix N Ablations: Variance Reduction in Strategy-Aware RL

In our theoretical formulation of the Compute Aligned Training framework for Reinforcement Learning (Appendix B), the pure policy gradient estimator applies a weight directly proportional to the marginal increase in test-time success: wRL=∂p~∂pw_{\text{RL}}=\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p}. However, as analyzed in Section B.6 and Section B.7.1, this pure estimator can suffer from severe variance inflation, particularly for strategies like Pass@NN evaluated at large NN.

To remedy this, our primary RL implementation utilizes an normalization mechanism derived from the SFT framework, multiplying the raw weight by a normalization term pp~\frac{p}{\tilde{p}} to create a "Log-Weighted" estimator. We discussed some motivation for this in Section B.7.1 .

To empirically validate the necessity of this stabilization term, we conducted an ablation study utilizing the Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) pipeline. We compared models trained with the pure RL weights against those trained with the Log-Weighted formulation across training budgets N∈{4,16}N\in\{4,16\}.

N.1 Empirical Results

The full test-time scaling results of this ablation are detailed in Table 13 and visualized in Figure 19.

Standard RL vs. Strategy-Aware RL:

All strategy-aware models, regardless of the specific weighting formulation, demonstrate superior scaling properties compared to the Standard RL baseline. Standard RL saturates quickly, reaching only 35.80%35.80\% at k=32k=32, validating our hypothesis that mean-seeking objectives inadvertently suppress the distributional variance required for effective search.

Pure RL vs. Log-Weighted (Normalized):

The ablation clearly demonstrates the superiority of the Log-Weighted estimator, and highlights exactly when and why the Pure RL estimator fails:

  • •

    Low Budget (N=4N=4): When the training budget is small, the variance penalty of the Pure RL weight (N2=16N^{2}=16) remains manageable for the optimizer. Consequently, both Pass@4 and Pass@4 (Log) perform similarly, successfully optimizing for low-budget precision (k≤8k\leq 8).

  • •

    High Budget (N=16N=16): As the training budget scales, the instability of the Pure RL estimator degrades performance. The Pass@16 (Pure RL) model fails to eclipse the Pass@4 models, achieving only 37.20%37.20\% at k=32k=32. The unnormalized gradient magnitudes likely cause optimization thrashing, preventing the policy from smoothly reallocating probability mass to the tails.

  • •

    The Stabilized Champion: In contrast, the Pass@16 (Log) model effectively leverages the higher "mental budget." Guarded by the adaptive gain controller, it successfully trains on harder examples without destabilizing the policy, achieving the highest asymptotic performance of 40.00%40.00\% at k=32k=32 (a substantial +4.2%+4.2\% absolute improvement over Standard RL).

Ultimately, this ablation confirms that while aligning the RL objective with the test-time strategy provides the correct directional signal, stabilizing the magnitude of the estimator via the pp~\frac{p}{\tilde{p}} normalization term is practically essential for robust optimization at scale.

N.2 Ablation Study: SFT vs. RL Weighting in Majority Vote RL

To rigorously test the impact of the specific gradient estimator used during Reinforcement Learning, we conducted an ablation study comparing the standard SFT-derived weighting factor against our proposed RL-specific weighting factor.

While both approaches aim to align the objective with the test-time metric, they differ in their normalization. The SFT-derived weight, wS​F​T=pp~​∂p~∂pw_{SFT}=\frac{p}{\tilde{p}}\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p}, includes a normalization term pp~\frac{p}{\tilde{p}} designed to prevent variance explosion as p→0p\to 0. In contrast, the RL-specific weight, wR​L=∂p~∂pw_{RL}=\frac{\partial\tilde{p}}{\partial p}, is the raw marginal utility, which concentrates the gradient signal entirely on the decision boundary.

We trained models using both estimators across two different target budgets (N=4N=4 and N=8N=8). The results are visualized in Figure 20 and detailed quantitatively in Table 14.

Analysis.

The results confirm two key findings:

  1. 1.

    Superiority of RL Weights: The RL_Wt_Maj4 model achieves the highest asymptotic performance (23.00% at Maj@16), outperforming both the baseline and the SFT-weighted variants. This supports the hypothesis that the "spotlight" behavior of the raw derivative, which vanishes for easy/hard samples and explodes at the boundary,is a feature, not a bug, for consensus tasks.

  2. 2.

    The Trade-off: The SFT_Wt models (Blue/Orange) start slower (lower Maj@4) but scale robustly. Their normalized weights effectively reduce variance, but at the cost of "blurring" the critical decision boundary signal needed to maximize the plurality vote.
